New Delhi [India], October 15 (ANI): The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will come into force on October 20, while India and Canada are targeting the conclusion of negotiations for their proposed trade agreement by the end of 2026, as India seeks to expand market access for exporters amid global trade uncertainties.
According to a presentation by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday, India and Canada are aiming to conclude negotiations for their proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) by the end of 2026.
The fifth round of negotiations between the two countries was held in Ottawa from October 5 to 9, with discussions covering market access for goods and services, investment, rules of origin, intellectual property rights and trade remedies. The next round of talks is planned for early November in New Delhi.
The proposed agreement is expected to strengthen economic ties between the two countries by reducing trade barriers and improving market access for businesses.
Meanwhile, the India-New Zealand FTA, signed in April 2026, will become operational on October 20. The agreement will provide duty-free access to Indian exports entering New Zealand, creating opportunities for sectors such as textiles, leather, footwear, engineering goods and processed agricultural products.
These developments come as India's merchandise exports have recorded growth across several major trading partners during the first half of the current financial year.
According to the Commerce Ministry's trade data, India's exports to the United Kingdom increased to USD 7.32 billion during April-September 2026, from USD 6.83 billion a year earlier. The India-UK trade agreement came into force in July this year.
Exports to China also rose to USD 11.41 billion from USD 8.39 billion, while shipments to the European Union increased to USD 31.92 billion from USD 30.61 billion.
India has earlier concluded FTA negotiations with the European Union, although the agreement is yet to enter into force.
The ministry's presentation further showed that negotiations are underway with several other trading partners, including the United States, Israel, Chile and Peru.
India is also pursuing reviews or upgrades of existing trade agreements with Australia, ASEAN, South Korea and Sri Lanka.
The ongoing negotiations and implementation of new agreements are part of India's efforts to diversify export destinations and secure better market access for domestic businesses amid changing global tariff policies. (ANI)

articles.title: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: FM Nirmala Sitharaman - www.malaysiasun.com
articles.summary: Non-tariff barriers biggest hurdle in India-China trade: FM Nirmala Sitharaman  www.malaysiasun.com
articles.full_text:
ANI
                
16 Oct 2026, 11:32 GMT+10
            
New Delhi [India], October 16 (ANI): Non-tariff barriers remain the single biggest obstacle in trade ties between India and China, Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman said on Friday, pointing out that an expanding trade imbalance continues to weigh heavily against the country despite years of bilateral engagement.
The Minister made these observations during an interactive session with Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council on 'India's economic edge', held on the sidelines of the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
Addressing the trade friction with Beijing, Sitharaman said that, "So non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China. That is one, and second, if the approach globally that you see today, where imbalance is huge, countries impose tariffs and say, 'no, we cannot sustain this imbalance, either you correct it or else we are going to be very punitive on you', that approach we have never taken."
Sitharaman mentioned that with China, the trade balance is against India' and it is growing exponentially. "The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking about with China now for several years. We are denied market access, even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China."
She noted that Indian products face persistent roadblocks across key sectors despite proven global competitiveness.
"We are global leaders in generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and perishables and very many such goods which have huge potential in China. I would think a decade has gone by, consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products. But non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly, whether it is in the name of phytosanitary measures or any other, for which due investigations can happen, for which due both sides sitting and talking can happen, but no progress is made," the Minister said.
Highlighting India's distinct approach to resolving trade frictions through dialogue rather than sudden retaliatory tariffs, she added that "it is not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome. But we do go through that approach rather than put CVDs, countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter the non-tariff barriers on the other side. So these are ways in which we find it difficult to correct the imbalance which prevails between China and us."
Beyond bilateral relations with China, the Finance Minister also touched upon the much anticipated India-US trade agreement.
"I think recently, a day or two ago, the Indian Commerce Minister has also spoken that they expect and wish to have the [India-US] agreement signed soon. Negotiations have been going on, I hope, in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners, India and US, the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest," she noted.
Sitharaman also reiterated India's commitment to multilateralism while actively pursuing direct trade agreements with key partners, including the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Canada, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, alongside ongoing efforts to finalize a pact with the United States. (ANI)

Hello and welcome to The Core Report special edition.
I am joined today by Rahul Mithal, Chairman and Managing Director of RITES.
Let's find out more about the company, what it does, and why some of the things RITES is focusing on right now, including detailed project reports, are so critical at this time.
Thank you so much for joining me.
I am going to come to DPRs, or Detailed Project Reports, in a while, because that is really the foundation of everything you do.
But before that, tell us about what RITES does and how it was set up, for those who don't know.
Good morning.
RITES is a 52-year-young company.
It has a unique position in the infrastructure consultancy market: we are the only company in India, whether in the PSU space or the private infrastructure consultancy space, that has all areas of infrastructure under one roof, whether it is railways, ports, airports, highways, buildings, etc.
We have 13 different verticals, and we do three kinds of work primarily.
One is the DPR, the techno-economic feasibility report.
The second is project supervision, when the project is actually happening.
The third is third-party technical audits.
This 3-by-13 matrix makes us well equipped.
We are executing about 700-plus orders today, in the country and beyond.
We can proudly say that we are a one-order-a-day company, with a fresh order inflow of one order a day.
About 70–75% of these are on a competitive basis, both domestic and global.
When RITES was set up, it was obviously a subset of the Indian Railways, and you are also a railway man, so to speak.
Tell us about the breakup of orders today, both existing and current, between railway or railway-linked orders and non-railway orders.
Yes.
When RITES was incorporated in 1974, it was, and still is, a company with majority holding by the Ministry of Railways, so traditionally rail infrastructure consultancy was our core sector.
But very soon, right in the first decade, the founders had the vision and foresight to make RITES a core consultancy company across all sectors.
We started working with the Delhi Metro, and we were the initial consultants for it.
The Mumbai-Pune Expressway was one of the first highways, and RITES was the consultant for that.
Within the first year itself, we started doing international projects.
As I said, the railway sector accounts for about 30–35–40% of my total top line and bottom line.
But sectors like buildings, ports, airports and highways are also very important verticals for us, and they contribute to both revenue and bottom line.
How have things been shaping up in the last couple of years, given the geopolitical shifts we are seeing, particularly when it comes to global orders? I know you have been talking about consistency in orders from the Middle East despite all the trouble there.
And how has it been evolving in India, which of course has been seeing huge capital expenditure as a country? About two to two and a half years back, we were at about 0.
6 orders a day.
Gradually, market competition became much higher, and the era of giving PSUs work on a nomination basis was receding.
Our business re-engineering and our experience of 50-plus years made us very well equipped, and that is why we stepped up from 0.
6 to about one order a day.
We are now steadily maintaining that strike rate.
In some geographies there are ups and downs once in a while, but we still continue to get orders, both domestically and internationally.
In fact, we have pushed our international business arm, which covers both design and export of rolling stock as well as project consultancy.
In the last year we have opened five regional offices across various geographies of the world: Latin America, West Asia, two regions in the African continent, and one in Southeast Asia, in Manila.
That is the kind of push we have given to our international business.
If I were to ask you about this financial year, starting April 2026 as a start point, or even calendar year 2026, what would be the three or four most interesting projects that RITES has secured, whether in India or globally?Let me tell you about two or three key projects across my verticals.
In the rail infrastructure vertical, we are doing the feasibility study for a new high-speed corridor, the Chennai–Bangalore–Hyderabad high-speed corridor.
That is very exciting.
We had been associated with the earlier high-speed corridor, Mumbai–Ahmedabad.
We are also doing a lot of work in the metro sector.
While we were doing the Ahmedabad Metro and the Bangalore Metro, we most recently got the order for the Patna Metro.
We are also doing feasibility studies for metros across various geographies, for new metro corridors that are getting announced.
There is also the push for educational institutions like the IITs and IIMs, and we are proudly associated with premier institutions.
We are doing the expansion of IIT Delhi, IIM Bangalore, IIM Raipur and IIT Bhilai.
That is the kind of work we are doing in the building sector.

Narayan said the amount was not tied to a fixed investment timetable and would depend on the outcome of bids.
"We are prepared to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion (in India)," he told a select group of journalists.
DP World, which has built an integrated Indian network spanning ports, rail and inland logistics, is seeking to expand its footprint as the world's most populous country looks to strengthen domestic connectivity and become a larger manufacturing and export hub.
The company announced an additional $5 billion India investment commitment in October 2025, over and above $3 billion invested in the country over three decades.
India's infrastructure push has delivered substantial improvements, Narayan said, but port and rail development and the processes governing project execution need to move faster.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, pointing to the long wait for the Vadhavan project and arguing that infrastructure development should keep pace with progress in roads, airports and power.
DP World is prepared to bid for new opportunities, expand its rail network and increase port capacity, Narayan said. The company currently operates six port concessions in India and plans to increase its railheads from eight to 12, according to him.
India's growing economic scale makes it attractive despite historically weaker returns on invested capital, Narayan said. Currency depreciation, driven in part by the country's energy import bill, has weighed on returns, while infrastructure upgrades, digitisation and the shift towards renewable energy could improve the outlook.
The proposed investment would also help strengthen DP World's wider supply-chain network, rather than simply expand its Indian business, he said.
The investment push comes as disruptions around key West Asian maritime chokepoints force shipping companies to reroute cargo, add capacity and absorb higher operating costs.
Narayan said DP World's flagship Jebel Ali port in Dubai, which normally handles about 15 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) annually, was facing a severe reduction in activity because of restricted access. He said the disruption was affecting cargo flows well beyond the Gulf, creating congestion at ports and logistics facilities across parts of Asia and Africa.
The impact extends beyond the port itself, he said, because Jebel Ali serves as a major transshipment hub linking Asian manufacturing centres with markets in the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
DP World had expected Jebel Ali's port operations to generate about $1.2 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), but Narayan said the disruption would materially reduce the group's earnings outlook. He estimated that global EBITDA could fall to about $5.8 billion from a level of roughly $6.2 billion to $6.4 billion, with growth elsewhere cushioning part of the lost contribution.
The company is exploring alternative routes through other Gulf ports and overland connections, including routes through Saudi Arabia, Narayan said. But building replacement capacity takes time, and he estimated that new port capacity could take two to three years to develop.
"Port capacity is not created overnight," he said, warning that the full consequences of the disruption may take time to emerge.
The crisis also underscores the growing cost of building redundancy into supply chains. Companies that once prioritised lean inventories, low costs and just-in-time deliveries are increasingly seeking alternative suppliers, routes and production centres to reduce their exposure to geopolitical shocks.
Narayan said global trade now required substantially more shipping capacity to move less cargo than before, as longer routes and operational inefficiencies absorbed available capacity. Higher interest rates, fuel expenses and other operating costs were adding to the burden.
"Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You - as a consumer," he said, arguing that the additional costs would ultimately be passed through to buyers of goods.
He expects shorter supply chains and a greater emphasis on regional production to reshape trade flows over time, potentially increasing the importance of north-south trade between Asia, Africa and other emerging markets.
For India, the opportunity lies in expanding manufacturing and exports while building the port, rail and inland logistics infrastructure needed to connect producers with global markets.
Narayan said India's exports and imports currently account for a relatively small share of its overall economy, leaving considerable room for growth. A substantial increase in trade would require a corresponding expansion in logistics capacity, he said.
However, he cautioned that resilience would come at a cost. Maintaining alternative routes, suppliers and inventory buffers would make supply chains more expensive and capital-intensive than the lean systems businesses had previously pursued.
"The world has to come to peace," Narayan said, arguing that physical infrastructure alone cannot eliminate the risks posed by conflict.

articles.title: DP World ready to invest up to $5 billion in India, but infrastructure projects need to move faster: CEO - Moneycontrol.com
articles.summary: DP World ready to invest up to $5 billion in India, but infrastructure projects need to move faster: CEO  Moneycontrol.com
articles.full_text:
Global logistics major DP World is prepared to invest another $3–5 billion in India across ports, railways and logistics infrastructure, but the country needs to accelerate project approvals and infrastructure development to fully capitalise on its economic potential, Group CEO Yuvraj Narayan said.
DP World eyes port and railway expansion
Narayan said DP World remained committed to expanding its Indian operations and was prepared to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion across ports, railways and logistics infrastructure.
"We are prepared to invest between $3 to $5 billion. But these are all bids, right? So, the best we can do is bid," he said.
The company has six port concessions in India and is looking to expand its network. Narayan said DP World currently has eight railheads, with plans to increase the number to 12.
The company is also interested in bidding for opportunities at Vadhavan port, which Narayan estimated could involve around $10 billion of investment across different phases over 10–15 years.
Narayan indicated that DP World currently had around $2.5 billion invested in India and that further investments could eventually take the country's share of the group's global invested capital to around 10–12 percent.
Rupee depreciation to cost more
Narayan said depreciation of the rupee had significantly eroded returns on the company's Indian investments, making the country one of its lower-return markets. However, he expects the investment outlook to improve as India reduces its dependence on imported energy, expands renewable energy capacity and strengthens its logistics infrastructure.
"The foreign currency piece in India has been what has destroyed returns," Narayan said, identifying currency depreciation as a major challenge for dollar-denominated investors.
"If you see what is destroying India's returns today, if it is the depreciation of the rupee, why is the rupee depreciating? It's because of your import of energy," he said.
He added that India's transition towards renewable energy could eventually ease pressure on the currency and improve investment returns.
Infrastructure needs to move faster
While acknowledging significant improvements in India's infrastructure over the past decade, Narayan said the pace of project implementation needed to accelerate, particularly in ports and railways.
"One always hopes things could happen faster," he said, adding that both regulatory processes and infrastructure development needed to be expedited.
"How long have we been talking about Vadhavan? Ever since I remember. So, it needs to happen quickly," he said, referring to the proposed deep-water port in Maharashtra.
Narayan said India had made substantial progress in expanding roads, airports, railways and digital infrastructure, but its ambition to become a major manufacturing and export hub would require significantly greater logistics capacity.
"As long as India is producing for India, for that you need internal connectivity. So that infrastructure investment is very well placed. The focus of the government today is to now start producing for the world. Therefore, connectivity to the rest of the world will become very important," he said.
He also questioned the complexity of infrastructure tendering, arguing that excessive emphasis on procedural compliance could delay project execution.
"When governance overtakes, becomes the primary objective, rather than getting a job done... the nation suffers," he said.
India's return profile set to change
Despite historically lower returns, Narayan expressed confidence that India's investment attractiveness would improve as its economy expanded and infrastructure strengthened.
"The whole return profile is going to change. As I said, today it's about resilience. And it's about scale. India is changing," he said.
He pointed to India's digitisation, infrastructure development and economic reforms over the past decade as reasons for the company's continued interest in the market.
"I think what India has achieved in terms of change and reform in the last 10 years is what gives us hope in the future," Narayan said.
He also left open the possibility of listing DP World's businesses on Indian exchanges in the future, particularly if the financial ecosystem at GIFT City became more closely integrated with domestic markets.
"If GIFT City becomes aligned with NSE, then it becomes a real possibility," he said.

articles.title: Bangladesh overtakes India in per capita GDP, but IMF sees India regaining lead in FY29 - The Business Standard
articles.summary: Bangladesh overtakes India in per capita GDP, but IMF sees India regaining lead in FY29  The Business Standard
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh had previously maintained a higher GDP per capita than India for seven consecutive years from 2018, before India overtook it in 2025.
Bangladesh's GDP per capita surpassed India's in FY26 and is projected to remain higher for the next two fiscal years, but the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects India to regain the lead in FY29 and widen the gap through FY31.
In its latest World Economic Outlook database, released on Tuesday, the IMF puts Bangladesh's GDP per capita in current US dollar at $2,886 in FY26, compared with $2,750 for India—a difference of just $136.
Despite having an economy roughly eight times larger, India is projected to stay behind Bangladesh until FY28. The forecast shows India's GDP per capita rising to $3,662 in FY29, surpassing Bangladesh's $3,334.
By FY31, the gap is expected to widen to around $709, with India's figure projected to reach $4,389 and Bangladesh's $3,680.
Bangladesh had previously maintained a higher GDP per capita than India for seven consecutive years from 2018, before India overtook it in 2025.
GDP per capita is calculated by dividing a country's total economic output by its population. It is commonly used to compare average economic output per person, although it does not directly measure how income is distributed or the cost of living.
India retains a lead in purchasing power
The picture changes when differences in living costs are taken into account.
India remains ahead of Bangladesh in GDP per capita measured at purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts for differences in the prices of goods and services between countries.
According to the IMF database, India's GDP per capita in PPP terms is projected at $12,998 in FY26, compared with $10,884 for Bangladesh, giving India a 19.4% advantage.
India has remained ahead on this measure every year since 1994, and the IMF expects it to retain that position through 2031, with the gap widening to around 45%.
Moreover, despite Bangladesh's projected lead in GDP per capita at current prices, India is expected to remain South Asia's fastest-growing economy over the forecast period.
Its GDP is projected to rise from $4.06 trillion in FY26 to $6.74 trillion in FY31, with annual growth forecast at 7.02% in FY27 and 6.81% in FY31.
Bangladesh, by contrast, is projected to record the region's slowest economic growth. Its annual growth rate is forecast to fall to 2.21% in FY28 before recovering to 2.97% by FY31.
The projections also place Bangladesh's ambition of becoming a $1 trillion economy by 2034 well above the IMF's current estimates. The Fund puts the country's GDP at $506.4 billion in FY26 and projects it to reach $674.4 billion by FY31.
Maldives leads in South Asia
Bangladesh also remains behind several other South Asian economies in GDP per capita.
The Maldives is projected to have the region's highest figure in FY26, at $19,507, followed by Sri Lanka at $5,062 and Bhutan at $4,933.
Pakistan's GDP per capita is estimated at $1,836, while Nepal is projected to have the region's lowest figure, at $1,540.

Ukraine has run out of missiles for its US-made Patriot air defence systems, leaving it vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks, CNN reported citing a source familiar with the situation.
The shortage comes amid mounting pressure on US weapons stocks, tensions between Washington and Kyiv over attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, and uncertainty over continued American military support.
According to CNN, Ukraine's shortage of Patriot interceptors left almost all Russian ballistic missiles in the latest overnight attack unintercepted.
The strikes hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring 25 in the Ukrainian capital. The shortage has raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to protect critical infrastructure as Russia continues its attacks on the country's energy network.
The interceptors are expensive and in short supply globally, with countries depleting their stockpiles or seeking to replenish their air defence systems amid the ongoing war involving Iran. The shortage has intensified concerns over Washington's ability to meet Ukraine's requirements while addressing its own military needs and those of its allies.
The shortage has coincided with a sharp deterioration in relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, following Washington's controversial deal to import Russian diesel and Trump's push for an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv.
Zelenskyy has accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite Kyiv temporarily halting strikes on Russian oil facilities in response to the proposal.
The dispute has extended beyond weapons supplies to US intelligence and satellite communications. Ukrainian officials told CNN they had not received the early-warning alerts about Russian ballistic missile launches that had previously helped authorities warn civilians to seek shelter.

articles.summary: Debt-strapped Pakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards of governors in 2027  India TodayPakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards next year for first time since 1953  The HinduPakistan to chair IMF, World Bank boards in 2027; first time in over 70 years  The Times of IndiaWhat does assuming the chairmanship of the IMF, World Bank governing boards mean for Pakistan?  DawnPakistan to chair World Bank, IMF Boards in 2027  CGTN
articles.full_text:
The Pakistani government called the appointment a "historic milestone", saying it would allow Islamabad to contribute to global economic discussions and facilitate dialogue among member countries. The diplomatic recognition, however, comes alongside a continuing need for external financing.
Pakistan is awaiting approval for another $1.2 billion from the IMF, yet the repeat borrower will chair the Boards of Governors of the IMF and World Bank Group in 2027.
The role puts the country in charge of proceedings attended by member countries’ finance ministers and central bank governors, giving Islamabad a prominent platform but no control over lending decisions.
Pakistan will hold the chairmanship for the first time since 1953, its Ministry of Economic Affairs said on Friday.
Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema, Pakistan’s governor to the World Bank, was announced as the incoming chair for 2027 during the World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
The ministry called the appointment a “historic milestone”, saying it would allow Pakistan to contribute to global economic discussions and facilitate dialogue among member countries. For Islamabad, however, the diplomatic recognition comes alongside a continuing need for external financing.
A BORROWER AT THE HEAD OF THE TABLE
Pakistan has entered into at least 25 IMF loan programmes since joining the institution in 1950. Its repeated returns to the lender reflect persistent difficulties in securing enough foreign currency to meet external obligations, compounded by inflation and financing pressures.
It is currently supported by a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) for economic reforms and external payment needs, alongside a $1.4 billion Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) to address climate-related risks.
The latest staff-level agreement could unlock about $1 billion under the EFF and $210 million under the RSF, taking total disbursements under both programmes to about $5.7 billion. It requires IMF Executive Board approval and covers the fourth EFF review and third RSF review, following talks led by the Fund’s Iva Petrova.
The World Bank has described Pakistan’s growth model, marked by high public consumption, low productivity and heavy borrowing, as unsustainable. The longer-term test is whether these loans can support growth that reduces the need for another bailout.
STABILITY RETURNS, DEPENDENCE REMAINS
The latest IMF assessment offers signs of improvement. The lender said Pakistan had preserved macroeconomic stability despite the West Asia conflict, helped by strong policies and support under its loan programme.
Real GDP grew 4 per cent in the first three quarters of FY26. Higher energy prices and supply disruptions then weakened momentum, leaving full-year growth estimated at 3.6 per cent.

articles.title: What is making BJP caution people about Bangladesh-like regime-change bid in India - India Today
articles.summary: What is making BJP caution people about Bangladesh-like regime-change bid in India  India Today
articles.full_text:
Lawyer-activist Prashant Bhushan's remarks on regime change and AISA leader Neha Bora's statement that Bangladesh has "shown us the way" have given the BJP ammunition to accuse the Congress and its allies of pursuing a Bangladesh-style regime change in India.
Talk of "regime change" has entered India's political discourse at a time when protests over alleged electoral irregularities have brought thousands onto Delhi's streets. The CJP, left-wing student groups and civil society bodies are demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's removal, while the Congress is running its own campaign against alleged "vote theft". Amid the stir, the BJP has launched a scathing attack on the Congress, accusing it of misleading the youth and attempting to create anarchy to bring about regime change in India.
The BJP has also warned of an attempt to replicate Bangladesh's 2024 protests, which forced PM Sheikh Hasina out of power. The BJP's concerns have been triggered by AISA chief Neha Bora's praise for Bangladesh's anti-Sheikh Hasina protests and senior advocate Prashant Bhushan's public endorsement of "regime change". The ruling party has linked these statements to Rahul Gandhi and the Opposition-backed protests demanding the removal of Gyanesh Kumar. It all began as an agitation over SIR and Gyanesh Kumar. Now, there's a raging political battle. Are the protesters defending India's democracy as they claim, or are they seeking to destabilise an elected government, as the BJP is claiming?
The trigger was Bhushan's statement at a joint press conference in Delhi on Thursday, October 15, a day before the CJP planned Tricolour march. On Friday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh led the BJP's attack on the Congress, accusing it and its allies of encouraging Bangladesh-style regime change through street mobilisation.
The BJP has also targeted YouTuber Dhruv Rathee over his remarks concerning the Army and police, with BJP MP Sambit Patra saying, "There can be no bigger anti-national than him."
Meanwhile, Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera mocked Rajnath Singh as "Jagga Jasoos" and "Sherlock Holmes", saying the Opposition had openly declared its goal of regime change through elections, just as happened in 1977 after the Emergency.
"Every time an opposition comes out on the streets, there is a movement, there is a regime change," said Khera, explaining that the Opposition sought regime change through elections.
The row comes against the backdrop of police action against protesters, disputes over the SIR of electoral rolls and growing political mobilisation involving students, lawyers and Opposition parties. Allegations of foreign influence have come from the BJP's highest ranks. Its national president, Nitin Nabin, has accused the Congress and the CJP of acting at the behest of foreign powers. So, where did the talk of regime change begin, who said what to fuel the controversy, and how has the BJP responded with accusations of a Bangladesh-style attempt to destabilise the Narendra Modi government?
WHAT DID PRASHANT BHUSHAN SAY ABOUT REGIME CHANGE?
At a Thursday press conference at New Delhi's Press Club of India, Prashant Bhushan appeared alongside CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, AISA president Neha Bora, Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal, actor Prakash Raj and other activists. The meeting was convened to address alleged electoral irregularities in the Election Commission, police action against protesters and demands for CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
"This government keeps on saying this is the opposition's operation of regime change. We are only appealing to save the electoral democracy in this country. If such barbarism continues, there will definitely be a regime change. We all want a regime change. Is there anything wrong with that? Regime change is a democratic right of every citizen, and creating disaffection against the government is not an offence," Bhushan said, defending the constitutional right to seek a change of "regime."
"We all want regime change. Getting regime change is every citizen's constitutional right," he added.
His remarks gave the BJP an opportunity to argue that the anti-SIR and anti-CEC protests' objectives are beyond just electoral reforms.
HOW BANGLADESH ENTERED THE CONTROVERSY
A comparison of the protests in India with Bangladesh's anti-Sheikh Hasina agitation of 2024 had already gained traction before Bhushan's remarks. On October 14, AISA president Neha Bora praised Bangladesh's 2024 anti-Shekh Hasina protests in a video message to the sixth national conference of the country's Socialist Students' Front. Bora was among those who went on a hunger strike at Jantar Mantar demanding Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation as Union Education Minister.
"We know that the Gen Z movement that we are seeing in India first started in Bangladesh. Congratulations to you for showing us the way," Bora said. "We extend our solidarity to you. We take inspiration from you, lessons from the movements that you lead," Bora added.
Her remarks were circulated on X by BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari on the same day.
"Neha Bora, Rahul Gandhi's poster girl says 'Bangladesh showed us the way' for the Revolution! This is Open Admission to Regime Change! Rahul Gandhi & Co are a threat to Indian Democracy!" Bhandari said, a day after the AISA leader from JNU appeared in a joint press conference with the Lok Sabha LoP.
Bangladesh's student-led protests began in July 2024 over government job quotas, but a deadly crackdown, mass arrests and internet shutdowns turned the agitation into a nationwide movement demanding Sheikh Hasina's resignation. On August 5, protesters, reportedly backed by Islamists and foreign forces, marched towards Dhaka in a final push that forced Hasina to flee to India, ending her 15-year rule.
Bora presented the Bangladesh protests as an inspiration for struggles over democratic and voting rights. The BJP interpreted the reference as an endorsement of the methods that removed Hasina from office.
Meanwhile, on social media, allegations that the Ford Foundation and the CIA are also involved in the regime change bid, have added another dimension.
BJP SEES BANGLADESH-STYLE REGIME-CHANGE PLOT BEHIND CONGRESS, CJP PROTESTS
The BJP sees Prashant Bhushan's and Neha Bora's remarks as part of a larger pattern involving CJP protests, Left-wing student mobilisation and Congress's "vote theft" campaign against the Election Commission. The BJP's attacks point to its wider allegation that these protests, coupled with criticism of constitutional institutions and references to Bangladesh's protests, are part of a coordinated attempt to destabilise the Modi government through street unrest.
On October 15, spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari alleged that Bora's comments reflected the thinking of Rahul Gandhi and his political associates. "This is an open admission of regime change. Rahul Gandhi and Co. are a threat to Indian democracy!" Bhandari wrote on X.
The party argued that attempts to undermine confidence in the Election Commission, combined with mobilisation on Delhi's streets, could create conditions resembling Bangladesh's political turmoil.
A day later on October 16, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh escalated the BJP's attack at a press conference in Lucknow. Singh accused Congress and its allies of using young protesters to create political instability. "The young of the country are being made pawns in the politics of anarchy," he said.
RAJNATH SINGH LEADS BJP'S CHARGE; TOP LEADERS ATTACK CONGRESS OVER REGIME-CHANGE
Rajnath Singh argued that the references to Bangladesh and regime change indicated an agenda extending beyond the SIR controversy. He accused the Opposition of attempting to dismantle democratic institutions and said political change must respect constitutional processes.
"India's future is everyone's responsibility. We must choose the path of dialogue and nation-building, not confrontation," Singh said.
His attack amplified the BJPs' charge on the Congress and the CJP without naming them much. Now it was time for the government's senior-most ministers and the BJP's top leadership.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis also attacked the protesters, saying, "After all, it was all about Regime Change." He alleged that the objective was to grab power by provoking students and farmers, spreading hatred along caste and linguistic lines, and tarnishing the image of constitutional institutions. "Spreading anarchy under the guise of a movement is precisely their objective," he wrote on X.
Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant also accused the Opposition of pursuing a "regime-change agenda", saying Prashant Bhushan's remarks raised questions about whether political change was being sought through elections or "extra-constitutional agitation". Invoking Prime Minister Narendra Modi, he said the path to power lay in winning public trust and securing an electoral mandate. "In India, governments are changed by the people through the ballot, not by force or by bypassing the Constitution," Sawant wrote on X.
BJP MP Sambit Patra said, "Prashant Bhushan stated that this struggle is about regime change. Let me be very clear. This country is not anyone's private property. It does not belong to any single family. It belongs to 1.4 billion people. When they say they are fighting for regime change, it confirms what the BJP and ordinary citizens of this country have been saying all along. The true intent of Rahul Gandhi and his associates has nothing to do with the SIR issue, nor are they fighting for the future of our children."
BJP leader and Rajya Sabha MP Vinod Tawde alleged that the use of the term "regime change" made it clear that the Congress and Opposition's agitation was not about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, but a conspiracy to seize power by creating "anarchy" in the country.
In a way, Neha Bora's and Prashant Bhushan's remarks have handed the BJP fresh ammunition in a controversy that had centred on the SIR and demands for CEC

Connaught Place was heavily fortified as police and paramilitary forces cracked down on demonstrations linked to a planned Tiranga rally. Protesters carrying the national flag faced detention across Central Delhi, including student leaders Neha Bora and Dipankar Bhattacharya marching from Mandi House. Authorities shut Central Park for two days and deployed extensive security to prevent unauthorised gatherings, while maintaining regular metro services and traffic flow. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken into preventive custody from the residence of NCP SP spokesperson Anish Gawande after Delhi Police denied permission for his demonstration. Police served notices prohibiting the rally, citing concerns over public order, though Dipke argued that unfurling the national flag was peaceful and constitutional. Continued attempts by demonstrators to converge at the inner circle of Connaught Place led to sustained police action and reignited debate concerning democratic assembly rights.
Rajnath Singh Hits Out at Congress Over Protests, Alleges 'Regime Change' Plot Like Bangladesh
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh mounted a sharp attack on the Congress party and its allies, alleging that they are attempting to incite anarchy and orchestrate a 'regime change' in India modelled on events in Bangladesh. Addressing a press conference in Lucknow, he claimed the opposition is using youth-led demonstrations against the Election Commission of India and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as pawns in a politics of confrontation rather than pursuing genuine electoral reforms. He stated that the opposition's goal is to destabilise democratic institutions and seize power by creating chaos. Outlining past historical actions of the Congress, he pointed to the 1975 Emergency, the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, and actions against kar sevaks in 1990 as unforgivable offences, accusing the party of continuing to attack constitutional values. He advised Rahul Gandhi to shun disruptive politics and introspect.
LATEST VIDEOS
A major political row has erupted over Dr Seema Khanna, the Election Commission of India's Director General of Information Technology, following remarks by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi questioning her presence in Dehradun. Khanna, who joined the poll body on deputation from the National Informatics Centre in 2025, oversees digital infrastructure including ECINet and ERONet. Concerns were raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi over whether Electoral Registration Officers had adequate software access to manage and correct voter lists independently. The Election Commission clarified Khanna was in Dehradun overseeing election preparedness for Uttarakhand's upcoming assembly polls, amid opposition scrutiny over voter data transparency.
The Delhi Police has denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site amid ongoing demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise. Protests have now been redirected to three alternative locations: Ramlila Maidan, the CBD Ground in Shahdara, and Burari Ground. However, two of these newly designated venues are situated significantly farther away from Parliament and central administrative offices, with CBD Ground approximately fourteen kilometres away and Burari Ground nearly twenty-three kilometres away. Moving demonstrations away from the corridors of power introduces logistical challenges, including massive crowd capacities ranging from fifteen thousand to eighty thousand people, expensive booking fees, and mandatory police clearance. Critics point out that shifting demonstrations far from the political centre may isolate demonstrators from policymakers, the media, and spontaneous public participation.
A debate unfolded over permission rules for public demonstrations in Bengaluru versus Delhi. Following restrictions placed on a Tiranga march in Bengaluru, Karnataka BJP spokesperson and former Police Commissioner Bhaskar Rao defended police decisions to disallow protests outside Town Hall, citing traffic disruption and High Court directives that designate Freedom Park as the sole protest venue. Rao maintained, 'Bangalore is a congested city', noting that rules apply uniformly to all political parties. Meanwhile, Congress spokesperson Ashprit Kadial accused the BJP of double standards regarding democratic demonstrations and questioned police clampdowns. The discussion evaluated whether municipal protest curbs represent legitimate administrative regulations or selective crackdowns.

India-US trade deal: 'Big items done', both sides close to pact, says Gor
US envoy Sergio Gor expresses confidence in finalising the India-US trade deal, saying key issues have been resolved
Listen to This Article
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor on Thursday said negotiations for a bilateral trade deal were moving at an "incredible pace", and the "big items are done", underlining that he was confident that both sides will get the pact through.
During an interactive session at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum here, Gor also echoed External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar's assessment of the progress in the proposed India-US trade pact, saying "we are very close to landing it".
Asked about the status of the negotiations, Gor said, "I won't like to get into too many details at this stage, and let the ministers announce that. But in the grand scheme of things, big items are done." "We're actively engaged... Within three weeks of arriving here, we announced a trade deal. The European Union trade deal took almost 20 years. So we're at an incredible pace, and I am confident that we will get it done," Gor said.
The India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) was successfully concluded in January after nearly 20 years of negotiation.
"We have been at it for a year-and-a-half. We are at an incredible pace, I would say almost an unheard of pace So I am confident that we will get it (the deal) done," Gor said.
Also Read
India has maintained that both sides remain engaged for a mutually beneficial bilateral trade agreement.
The two sides continue to engage to iron out differences on the proposed deal, and negotiations are heading towards a "landing point", Jaishankar had said at an earlier session at the Forum, noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remained unchanged.
Gor said, "We are getting there. I am confident that we will have a trade deal here, as you heard Dr Jaishankar say right on this stage, and we are very close to landing it." He was also asked about the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, and if there is any room for some sanctions relief or exemptions related to it for India.
"That is a decision for the president," Gor said, adding the legislation gives the US president that authority.
He has not imposed sanctions on any country yet. The bill was passed recently, and "he has to make a determination within the next 10 days or so, and I am sure we will see an announcement from the White House soon," Gor said.
On September 18, US President Donald Trump signed into law the 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026', which authorises him to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries buying Russian oil and gas, including China and India.
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, during his meeting with a bipartisan US Congressional delegation in Delhi, had conveyed India's "concerns" over the implications of the recently enacted Act on bilateral ties and the international energy market.
The US envoy also underlined that this was a "very complex trade deal".
A lot of smaller countries do not have "tens of thousands of points to figure out", he said.
"You are always going to have something, some small items New items develop constantly, new technology comes up, new issues arise, which is natural. A country like India with 1.4 billion people is a complex place, and so matching everything won't be done overnight. But the big picture, the big framework, the big items are done," the envoy said.
Gor's comments assume significance, as they come a few days ahead of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's upcoming visit to India.
The envoy also referred to a US Supreme Court ruling related to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
"The Supreme Court had ruled that law unconstitutional, so the administration had to go back and rework some of those," he said.
The comment was made in the context of the complexities involved in the proposed trade deal.
Gor also said that US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer and India's Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal are literally discussing the proposed trade deal down to smaller details.
"You have an unmatched market here for our companies You have 1.4 billion people. And American products are popular in India. The NBA (National Basketball Association, a professional basketball league in the US) has got a following here, and you don't even have a league yet.
"So, for the private sector to be able to come to India to compete, to have their foot in the door, you have a very pragmatic prime minister... That welcomes outside investment," Gor said.
"Pick any sector, and we're working together at it. If you look at defence, we have co-production happening here in India. If you look at IT, it's unmatched. Google, Microsoft, Adobe, Micron -- each one of them is opening data centres and chip manufacturing units here that work with our companies, hand in hand, in the US.
"So when a job is created in India, a counter job is created in the US. It is an incredible win-win situation that I would call unmatched. Not a lot of countries in the world have such limitless potential," he said.

Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.

articles.title: India-US trade deal nears finish line: EAM - Daily Pioneer
articles.summary: India-US trade deal nears finish line: EAM  Daily Pioneer
articles.full_text:
India and the United States are continuing negotiations to resolve outstanding differences over a proposed bilateral trade agreement, with talks moving toward a possible “landing point,” External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said ahead of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s anticipated visit to India.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Tuesday evening, Jaishankar said negotiations were progressing but declined to disclose details of the discussions.
“I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn’t be comfortable spilling the beans in public,” he said when asked about the status of the proposed trade deal. Jaishankar said India’s Commerce and Industry Minister, the US Trade Representative (USTR), and other officials were discussing how to resolve the remaining differences and move the agreement forward.
“I sense that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point,” he said.
India and the US have been negotiating a bilateral trade agreement since early 2025, seeking to address tariff-related tensions, reduce non-tariff barriers and expand market access. New Delhi seeks more favourable tariff terms for Indian exports than those offered by competing economies.
Jaishankar noted that the outcome would depend not only on the terms India and the US negotiate but also on the agreements Washington reaches with other competing economies. Earlier this month, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the two countries were working to finalise a bilateral trade agreement, though a deal was not imminent. He said both sides had identified the outstanding issues and were working to resolve them.
Jaishankar’s remarks came more than a week after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said negotiations on the trade deal had reached a “plateau”. The external affairs minister also discussed Washington’s changing approach to global economic engagement, saying the US was seeking to rebuild its manufacturing base and reset the terms of access to its domestic market.
“The US is today determined to re-industrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy,” he said, adding that tariffs were closely linked to these objectives. He noted that major economies around the world were negotiating with Washington in response to its evolving trade policy.
“We’re not alone in this. In our case, we are pretty far advanced in that process of negotiation,” Jaishankar said.
On the broader bilateral relationship, Jaishankar said the US was reassessing the terms of its alliances and treaty relationships, with the impact being felt particularly in Europe and, to some extent, East Asia. However, he distinguished India’s relationship with Washington from formal military alliances, describing the two countries as strategic partners. “We have many issues we are working on with the United States, but we don’t have an issue of the terms of alliance because we are not officially an ally,” he said.
“India is a country which has a strong strategic partnership with the US, but a strategic partnership is a partnership; it’s not an alliance,” he added. Jaishankar said India and the US have spent more than two decades identifying areas of convergence, shared interests, and common priorities, and that the fundamental basis of their relationship has not changed.
India-US relations have faced significant strain after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on Indian goods last year. Tensions were also heightened by US President Donald Trump’s claims about his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military confrontation in May 2025, which drew sharp reactions from Indian officials.
Disputes over US immigration policy and the decision to raise H-1B visa fees have further strained bilateral ties. Washington’s move to restrict a key green-card processing programme affecting major global technology companies, including Indian IT firms Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, has added to the concerns.
Against this backdrop, the proposed trade agreement remains a key test of the two countries’ ability to manage economic differences while preserving their broader strategic partnership. Jaishankar’s latest remarks suggest that, despite unresolved issues, both sides continue working toward an agreement.

articles.title: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: From India, another example of incentives linked to investment performance.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the context of increasingly fierce competition to attract foreign investment, India is linking incentives to revenue, domestic supply chains, and R&D activities. This approach is noteworthy as Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies to better align with project performance.
India is spending $7.5 billion, but not just to produce more phones.
On August 21, 2026, India announced the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme 2026 (MPMS), following the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme which ended on March 31.
During the four years of implementing the PLI (Private Partnership in the Mobile Industry), from 2022 to 2025, India's smartphone exports increased more than sevenfold, from $3.1 billion to $24.1 billion. By 2025, smartphones will become the country's largest export item. This result lays the foundation for India to move to the next phase in its mobile phone industry development strategy.
Instead of focusing solely on expanding manufacturing and assembly, India aims to become a global mobile phone manufacturing and export hub, while also integrating the domestic supply chain more deeply into the process. The MPMS (Mobile Manufacturing and Production Management System) is designed to link the growth of production and revenue for businesses with the use of domestically sourced components as well as design, research, and development (R&D) activities.
A notable aspect of MPMS is that support is determined based on the actual performance of the business. For large-scale manufacturers, the support amount is calculated based on the portion of revenue exceeding the standard revenue threshold. Businesses that reach a certain revenue threshold and continue to maintain growth will be eligible for support.
This mechanism also encourages businesses to increase their use of components sourced from the Indian market. Phones using domestically sourced components can receive an additional subsidy of up to 1.5%. These components include screens, cameras, phone casings, batteries, and charging cables.
Indian domestic brands are eligible for higher levels of support if they meet conditions regarding ownership structure, operational control, and intellectual property rights, while also establishing design and research centers within the country. Thus, the level of support depends not only on size and revenue growth but also on the extent of participation in the domestic supply chain, as well as design and R&D activities.
You may also like
To implement the MPMS, India has allocated 62,500 crore rupees, equivalent to approximately US$7.5 billion. The program spans five fiscal years, from 2026-2027 to 2030-2031, with grants determined based on business performance.
The design of the MPMS shows that India is not simply allocating resources to increase mobile phone production. By linking support levels to business results and specific business activities, the program simultaneously aims at three goals: expanding revenue, increasing the use of domestically sourced components, and bringing more design and R&D activities into India.
This also marks a shift after the PLI phase. While the previous phase contributed to the rapid expansion of smartphone production and exports, MPMS places greater emphasis on value creation and retention within the economy , through domestic supply chains and higher-tech activities.
What are the implications for Vietnam?
India's approach to linking support resources to business performance is particularly noteworthy in the context of increasing competition for investment among Asian economies, while Vietnam is also refining its investment incentive and support policies in line with Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy.
In a recent report, the Foreign Investment Agency of the Ministry of Finance noted that regional economies such as India, Malaysia , and Thailand are stepping up incentive packages to attract shifting capital flows, especially in strategic sectors like semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and renewable energy. This creates additional competitive pressure on Vietnam in attracting and retaining high-quality investment projects.
At the same time, the need to innovate the methods of investment incentives and support has been raised. Resolution 10 emphasizes the need to "gradually shift from traditional incentives to a support mechanism linked to the operational efficiency of projects."
You may also like
One of the tools Vietnam is using is the Investment Support Fund, established under Decree No. 182/2024/ND-CP. The fund aims to stabilize the investment environment; encourage and attract strategic investors and multinational corporations; and support domestic businesses in certain sectors requiring investment incentives. Businesses meeting the eligibility criteria can receive support for costs such as training, R&D, fixed asset investment, and the production of high-tech products.
The Investment Support Fund is designed for multiple sectors, rather than focusing on a specific industry like the MPMS. This difference highlights a noteworthy aspect of resource allocation. With the MPMS, India selects a specific industry, clearly defining desired outcomes, from revenue growth and domestic supply chain development to bringing design and R&D activities domestically, and then links support levels to each of those outcomes.
In the context of limited support resources and increasingly fierce competition for investment, the selection of priority sectors and the level of resource concentration have become crucial factors in policy design and implementation. Focusing more on a few industries and sectors with the potential to create high added value, form supply chains, and disseminate technology can help support resources have a more significant impact, rather than allocating them too broadly.
Besides leveraging the effectiveness of the Investment Support Fund under Decree 182 to retain investors and supply chains, in the face of fierce competition to attract investment, India's method of quantifying results to determine the level of support in the MPMS program provides valuable experience for Vietnam as it gradually shifts from traditional incentives to performance-based support mechanisms in the future.

articles.title: Tata Sons’ semiconductor bet focused on India’s long-term growth - Communications Today
articles.summary: Tata Sons’ semiconductor bet focused on India’s long-term growth  Communications Today
articles.full_text:
For Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran, the group’s bet on semiconductors is not about getting the numbers right over the next two or three years, but about investing in a sector that will be critical to India’s long-term growth.
He said the group’s experience had shown that investments made with the country’s needs in mind had consistently proved to be the right decisions.
“Whether we get semiconductor chips right or we get the numbers right in two-three years, that is not the point.
“Chips are going to be fundamentally required for domestic consumers,” Chandrasekaran said.
He was speaking at a panel discussion titled The End of Predictability at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026.
He said this investment philosophy had encouraged the Tata group to venture into the semiconductor and electronics sectors.
India’s global manufacturing opportunity
Underlining India’s opportunity in global manufacturing, he said the country had the talent and domestic market to become an important player in global supply chains.    			
“We have the talent, domestic market, we can play a part in every global supply chain.
“We need partnerships because we do not have all the technologies.”
He also cautioned that while companies must be willing to take risks, they should keep an eye on their balance sheets.
“You have to be careful, and keep an eye on the balance sheet.
“One cannot be reckless. We need to see where the demand is,” he said.
Tata Electronics is establishing a fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat, in partnership with Dutch company ASML Holding NV.
The company is also setting up a semiconductor facility in Assam, which is expected to produce 48 million chips a day.
Navigating global uncertainty
Asked how the current global uncertainty differed from past events, Chandrasekaran said this was the first time so many disruptions were occurring simultaneously.    			
These included geopolitical tensions, disruption from artificial intelligence, and commodity and supply-chain disruptions.
“At the same time the connected world is trying to decouple itself.
“And tackling all of these things now is unique,” he added.
He identified technology as a major near-term disruptor, particularly when it fell into the hands of bad actors, and pointed to the labour restructuring that would eventually follow.
“The other thing that I worry about is the war situation.
“We are opening a war in every situation, and nothing is getting closed,” he added.
Building business resilience
Chandrasekaran said businesses should build resilience into their operations rather than focus solely on efficiency in an unpredictable environment.    			
He argued that the two were not mutually exclusive.
“In a highly unpredictable, volatile environment, optimising for efficiency is definitely not the right thing,” he said.
“I believe that if you design for resilience in an unpredictable environment, actually you are optimising for efficiency.”
He cited shortages of magnets that could disrupt vehicle production and the cyberattack that affected Jaguar Land Rover, saying the company had lost almost six weeks of production due to the incident.
The group had also faced an air crash and supply-chain disruptions, he said, but still expected to deliver double-digit growth while maintaining margins.
He did not specify the period or provide financial projections to quantify the outlook.
Chandrasekaran said he had asked companies across the group to define resilience for their own businesses rather than adopt a single framework. Rediff

articles.title: India-US trade deal nears finish as Rubio heads to India - www.thehawk.in
articles.summary: India-US trade deal nears finish as Rubio heads to India  www.thehawk.in
articles.full_text:
Washington, Oct 17 (IANS) India and the United States are close to sealing the first part of a trade agreement, with dairy access the biggest remaining obstacle, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to India.
President Donald Trump on Friday signed an order implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act and waiving its tariffs on buyers of Russian oil.
At its core, the trade negotiation is an exchange: lower and predictable US tariffs on Indian goods in return for wider access for American products in India.
Under a framework announced in February, Washington cut its reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25 per cent to 18 per cent and removed an additional 25 per cent duty linked to India’s purchases of Russian oil. In return, India committed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on US industrial goods and a range of farm products, including tree nuts, fruit, soybean oil, wine and spirits.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday that the first tranche had been finalised and was in legal drafting, but that implementation would depend on clarity about India’s competitive advantage.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has said the talks are nearing a “landing point”. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on October 2 that a deal was not imminent.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday expressed hope that the India-US trade agreement would be concluded at the earliest, in the interest of global trade and bilateral economic ties.
India’s merchandise exports “surged 23% to $44.4 billion in September 2026, while the trade deficit narrowed,” the Consulate General of India in New York said on X on Friday.
Large Indian purchases of US goods, such as commercial aircraft, coking coal, gold, energy and defence equipment, are among the ways the gap could be narrowed.
For India, the energy stakes are practical. Its refineries are configured largely for medium sour crude, a grade that comes mainly from the Gulf and Russia. Lighter US crude and heavier grades can be blended in, but only up to a point. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted by the West Asia conflict, replacing Russian barrels quickly is difficult.
At the same time, India has turned sharply towards American gas. The US became India’s largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplier for the first time in the March-May quarter, according to Kpler data.
In August, the US supplied more than half of India’s liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) imports, though the UAE overtook it in September as Gulf cargoes rebounded.
Rubio travels to Samarkand, Mumbai and Jamnagar from October 17 (Saturday) to 22. He is scheduled to hold talks with EAM Jaishankar in Mumbai on October 20.
Rising fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections give Washington its own reasons to avoid sharp supply disruptions.

Mumbai, India – October 2026: IBM and MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), an initiative of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with plans to accelerate India’s deep tech startup ecosystem by enabling startups with access to IBM’s technology expertise, mentorship, enterprise engagement opportunities, skilling programs, and ecosystem development initiatives. 
The collaboration brings together MeitY Startup Hub’s nationwide innovation network and IBM’s enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and quantum computing expertise to help high potential startups build, validate and scale technologies for India and global markets. It complements IBM Ventures’ ongoing engagements in India by expanding pathways for enterprise technology startups to connect with customers, investors and industry experts.
Dr. Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO, MSH said, "India's startup ecosystem is emerging as a global engine for technology innovation. Through this collaboration with IBM, we aim to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities, foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat."
As part of this collaboration, startups will get access to IBM’s portfolio of enterprise technologies and innovation platforms to solve business use cases. This includes technical guidance and enablement on technologies such as IBM watsonx, an enterprise ready AI and data platform; IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises; IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty; technical orientation on IBM’s hybrid cloud, and quantum computing; and security and automation solutions.
Under the MoU, IBM and MSH will jointly explore initiatives that support startups across multiple stages of growth and across sectors such as banking, finance, government, industrial and more. The collaboration will focus on enterprise proof of concepts, sovereign AI innovation, open-source ecosystem development, founder mentorship, technical skilling and opportunities for startups to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors. A key priority will be identifying and nurturing promising innovators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, broadening access to India’s growing deep tech ecosystem.

It had installed around 800 MW under each of the two categories by September, according to Banga.

articles.summary: China signals readiness to address economic and trade issues with India  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
China has expressed its willingness to discuss economic and trade concerns with India, signalling an effort to strengthen commercial cooperation as the two Asian neighbours seek to improve bilateral relations. The statement followed discussions between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and India’s Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on trade and economic ties, according to official statements and reports published in September.
Yu Jing, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in India, said Beijing was ready to work with New Delhi to implement the consensus reached by the two countries’ leaders, expand mutually beneficial economic cooperation and address each side’s concerns in a balanced manner. The statement came amid continuing Indian concerns about trade imbalances and access for Indian businesses in the Chinese market.
The diplomatic engagement follows a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping on September 12, on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. According to the Indian government’s account, both leaders agreed that economic and trade concerns, including structural trade imbalances and supply-chain issues, needed attention. They also emphasised the importance of meaningful and predictable market access.
Trade figures underline the challenge. India imported approximately $131.6 billion worth of goods from China in the 2025-26 financial year, while its exports to China stood at about $19.5 billion, leaving a trade deficit of more than $112 billion, according to figures reported by The Economic Times. The gap has long been a source of concern for Indian policymakers seeking better export opportunities for domestic manufacturers and businesses.
The two countries have significant economic links, particularly in electronics, machinery, industrial components and other manufactured goods. Indian businesses rely on Chinese supplies for several production inputs, while New Delhi has sought to improve market access for Indian products and reduce vulnerabilities in supply chains.
China’s latest statement indicates a willingness to continue engagement, but it does not announce a specific trade agreement, tariff change or new market-access commitment. Any practical progress will depend on whether further discussions produce measurable steps to address the concerns raised by both sides.
The economic dialogue is also taking place alongside broader efforts to stabilise bilateral relations following years of tensions. In September, the two leaders reiterated the need to maintain peace along the border while pursuing cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
The next stage is expected to involve continued diplomatic and commerce-level engagement. Businesses will be watching for concrete measures on export access, supply-chain cooperation and trade barriers, which will determine whether the latest expressions of willingness translate into a more balanced economic relationship.
