MoSPI data reveals a 63% surge in national highway project awards. India sees robust growth across aviation, telecom, ports, railways, and power sectors.
Key Points
- National highway project awards jumped 62.9% to 2,236.3 km in April-September FY'27.
- Electronic toll collection transactions increased by 24.1%, with value up 11.7% in FY 2026-27.
- Significant growth was also recorded in civil aviation, telecommunications, ports, and railways sectors.
- The power sector saw a 12.1% increase in installed capacity, with renewables growing 29.5% to 42% of total capacity.
- The data comes from MoSPI's expanded PAIMANA Performance Dashboard, now monitoring 184 indicators.
This significant increase strengthens the pipeline of highway infrastructure development, paving the way for enhanced connectivity, improved logistics efficiency, and sustained economic growth, the ministry stated.
Road Transport and Highways sector continued to witness expansion in electronic toll collection, with such transactions increasing to 225.2 crore during FY 2026-27 (April-September), registering a year-on-year growth of 24.1 per cent.
Further, the electronic toll collection (ETC) value stands at Rs 36,994.5 crore for the same period with YoY growth of 11.7 per cent, indicating sustained adoption of electronic tolling and increasing digitalisation of toll collection across the road network. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) is releasing the quarterly update of the PAIMANA (Project Assessment, Infrastructure Monitoring & Analytics for Nation building) Performance Dashboard, presenting the performance of key infrastructure sectors through a set of standardised indicators.
The civil aviation sector recorded sustained growth in air cargo movement, with cargo handled up 12.0 per cent YoY during FY 2026-27 (April-August) to 18.6 lakh tonnes, indicating broad-based growth in air freight activity.
The civil aviation sector continues to support India's growing international tourism footprint, with 30.49 lakh foreign tourist arrivals recorded up to August in FY 2026â27, up 2 per cent YoY.
Telecommunication sector recorded continued expansion of digital infrastructure, with cumulative Optical Fibre Cable (OFC) laid reaching 7,52,113 km by August 2026.
This represents an addition of 29,256 km during FY 2026-27 (April-August), strengthening the country's high-speed digital connectivity infrastructure.
The number of Gram Panchayats connected also increased to 2,23,814 as of August 2026, representing addition of 5,352 in FY 2026-27 (April-August).
Ports, Shipping and Waterways sector recorded continued growth in cargo traffic, with cargo handled at Major Ports rising by 7.2 per cent YoY to 390.4 million tonnes during FY 2026-27 (April-August).
Cargo traffic at Non-Major Ports increased by 1.8 per cent YoY to 313.4 million tonnes during the same period.

articles.title: C-CAMP to get Rs 500-crore funding under Centre’s RDI Fund to back biotech Startups - The Times of India
articles.summary: C-CAMP to get Rs 500-crore funding under Centre’s RDI Fund to back biotech Startups  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
BENGALURU: The Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP), a Bengaluru-based biotech research and innovation organisation, has been selected as one of five Focused Research Organisations (FROs) under the Centre’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, with a funding commitment of Rs 500 crore to support deeptech innovation.
C-CAMP will work with private partners and investors to build a consortium with funding of more than Rs 1,000 crore — including the Rs 500 crore — to back deeptech life sciences startups developing technologies with potential for impact in India and globally.
It is the only dedicated biotechnology organisation among the 19 Second Level Fund Managers (SLFMs) announced under the initiative. The list comprises five FROs and 14 venture capital firms, with a combined allocation of Rs 7,131 crore. The other FROs are the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), IIT Bombay, IIT Madras and BITS Pilani.
C-CAMP aims to support high-risk, potentially transformative biotechnology innovations in healthcare, agriculture, food security and environmental sustainability.
Welcoming the announcement, C-CAMP Director-CEO Dr Taslimarif Saiyed said the selection would help bring more Indian deeptech startups closer to real-world impact. 
He said inadequate funding remained a major bottleneck for biotech innovators seeking to compete globally, and that C-CAMP would work to address this through its role as an RDI fund manager.
The RDI Fund, announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 3, 2025, is a Rs 1 lakh crore initiative spread over six years to increase private-sector participation in research and innovation. It aims to bridge the shortage of patient capital for high-risk, high-potential sectors such as deeptech.
Approved by the Union Cabinet on July 1, 2025, the fund has already supported 22 startups through direct project funding. Two of these — Eyestem Research and Peptris Technologies — are part of C-CAMP’s portfolio.
The fund’s eligibility criteria include technologies at Technology Readiness Level 4 and above, indicating development beyond the early laboratory stage and closer to practical application.
Saiyed said C-CAMP would focus on patient capital to nurture ideas as well as disciplined investment to help deep-science ventures develop commercially. Its network across the biotechnology ecosystem, he added, would help mobilise further private investment.

articles.title: India-US trade deal nears finish line: What the first tranche could mean for businesses - India Weekly
articles.summary: India-US trade deal nears finish line: What the first tranche could mean for businesses  India Weekly
articles.full_text:
Highlights:
India and the United States have finalized the first tranche of their proposed bilateral trade agreement, with legal drafting underway. The next step is to settle the terms and determine when the deal can be signed and implemented, potentially easing tariff tensions that have complicated trade between the two countries.
Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal announced the development on Thursday, October 15, saying India wants to secure tariff terms that put its exporters on a competitive footing against other countries selling goods in the US market.
"The US bilateral trade agreement first tranche has been finalised. It's going through final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get comparable advantage or competitive advantage over our peer countries," Goyal, addressing the SRCC Centenary Conclave in Delhi, said.
The announcement signals progress, but it does not mean the trade agreement is already signed or in force. The two governments must still complete the remaining work, including the legal process and the broader US tariff framework.
Why The US Tariff Structure Matters
India is seeking tariff treatment that allows its goods to compete more effectively with products from rival exporting countries. The final terms could influence how attractive Indian products are to American buyers, although the specific tariff rates and sectors covered by the first tranche have not yet been detailed in the announcement.
Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations were moving in the right direction and expressed hope that the agreement could be concluded soon.
"Probably we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing the deal at the earliest possible time," he told reporters.
However, he said the timing would depend partly on the United States formalizing its overall tariff structure.
"So there is a parallel work being done in the US also to get back the tariff structure and based on some of the outcomes under (Section) 301, we will progress towards signing the deal at a mutually agreed time," he said.
Section 301 of US trade law allows Washington to investigate and respond to certain foreign trade practices. The outcomes of the relevant US process could therefore affect how the agreement moves toward signing.
What The Deal Is Expected To Address
India and the US have been negotiating since early 2025, seeking to reduce tariff friction, address non-tariff barriers and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar also indicated that the negotiations were approaching a possible conclusion, while stressing the importance of comparing India's terms with those secured by competing economies.
"When countries negotiate with an economy like the United States, obviously one part of it is what you work out between yourselves and the US, and one part of it is how do you fare vis-a-vis competitive economies," Jaishankar said.
He added that the terms other countries secure remain an important consideration.
"My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point," Jaishankar added.
Why The Agreement Matters For India-US Relations
The trade negotiations have taken place against a backdrop of strained bilateral relations. Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India in 2025, while disagreements over President Donald Trump's claims about helping de-escalate the India-Pakistan military clashes in May 2025 drew sharp reactions from Indian officials.
Disputes over US immigration policy and higher H-1B visa fees have added to tensions. Washington's decision to restrict a key green-card processing program affecting major global and Indian IT firms, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, has created further friction.
A finalized trade agreement could provide a framework for improving commercial ties, but its immediate impact will depend on the final terms. For Indian exporters, the central question is whether the agreement delivers a meaningful tariff advantage. For businesses on both sides, the next milestones are the publication of the draft, completion of legal procedures and a mutually agreed signing date.
For now, the first tranche represents progress rather than a completed trade pact. The details of the agreement—and the competitive advantage India is seeking—will determine how significant that progress proves to be.

articles.title: Nirmala Sitharaman on India-China Trade Barriers - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: Nirmala Sitharaman on India-China Trade Barriers  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Ajay.K
Nirmala Sitharaman says China’s non-tariff barriers restrict Indian exports as the India-China trade deficit exceeds $100 billion in 2026.
Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has said that non-tariff barriers imposed by China are the biggest hurdle in India-China trade. Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, she highlighted the difficulties faced by Indian exporters seeking access to the Chinese market.
Sitharaman said India’s trade imbalance with China was growing and argued that restrictions on Indian products were preventing businesses from fully tapping the market’s potential.
China’s Trade Barriers Restrict Indian Exports
Sitharaman highlighted restrictions affecting several Indian products, including generic medicines, bovine meat and vegetables. She pointed to phytosanitary requirements and other regulatory measures that can delay or limit access to foreign markets.
Phytosanitary rules are designed to protect plants and agricultural products from pests and diseases. However, differences in regulatory requirements and delays in market-access approvals can create challenges for exporters.
According to the minister, India has continued to engage with China through discussions and negotiations to address these barriers, but progress has been slow in several areas.
India-China Trade Deficit Exceeds $100 Billion
The minister also expressed concern over India’s widening trade deficit with China. The trade deficit represents the difference between the value of goods India imports from China and the value of goods it exports to the country.
India’s trade deficit with China has crossed $100 billion so far in 2026, according to reports on her remarks. The imbalance highlights the gap between Indian demand for Chinese products and the market access available to Indian exporters.
Sitharaman said India had avoided responding with punitive trade barriers or countervailing duties, preferring negotiations to address the imbalance.
India Seeks Fairer Market Access
India has been seeking better access for its products in China, particularly in sectors where Indian businesses see export potential. Improving market access could create opportunities for pharmaceutical companies, agricultural exporters and other domestic industries.
The issue also reflects the wider challenge of balancing trade relationships when regulatory requirements and access conditions differ between countries.
India and China have taken steps to stabilise bilateral relations after tensions following the 2020 border clash. However, trade imbalances and restrictions on market access remain important economic concerns.
Finance Minister Calls for Early India-US Trade Deal
During the same interaction, Sitharaman also expressed hope that the proposed India-US trade agreement would be concluded at the earliest.
She said the agreement would be beneficial for bilateral economic ties and global trade. Her comments came after Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal indicated that the first phase of the India-US trade agreement had been finalised and was undergoing legal drafting.
The government is continuing discussions with trading partners to improve export opportunities while addressing concerns over market access and trade imbalances.
India Reviews Its Wider Trade Relationships
Sitharaman also raised concerns about India’s trade arrangements with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), describing the existing terms as unfavourable to India in some respects. She said India intended to maintain the agreement but believed its terms needed to be reviewed.
The remarks underline the government’s broader focus on securing more balanced trade relationships, improving access for Indian products and supporting domestic businesses in international markets.

articles.summary: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says  BBCVHP seeks release of Sri Lankan Hindu youth convicted of blasphemy in Saudi Arabia  ThePrintSaudi Supreme Court sets aside Sri Lankan migrant worker’s death penalty  The HinduHe must be released: Karti on Hindu man sentenced to death in Saudi | He had reportedly deleted the post & apologised | Inshorts  InshortsSaudi Arabia Overturns Death Sentence For Sri Lankan Man&nb...
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said.
Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment.
The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.
Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts.
In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court.
Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling.
Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September.
International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life.
"Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar's husband breaks silence after FBI raid on home; denies concerns over immigration probe - The Times of India
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's husband breaks silence after FBI raid on home; denies concerns over immigration probe  The Times of IndiaIlhan Omar Investigation Aims to Build Case for Stripping Her Citizenship  WSJUS probes Omar's decades-old immigration paperwork with eye toward deportation, sources say  ReutersWhat we know about the criminal investigation into US congresswoman Ilhan Omar  BBCTrump officials scrutinized Omar in 2019. They didn’t find citizenship issues.&nb...
articles.full_text:
Ilhan Omar’s husband, political consultant Tim Mynett, has spoken out after federal agents raided the Minnesota congresswoman’s Washington, DC, residence as part of a criminal investigation into her immigration records, while also addressing questions about her reported absence from public view.
Mynett was seen leaving the couple’s rented home on Wednesday to walk their golden Labrador, Teddy, and later to take out the trash, according to the New York Post. He was also seen accompanying one of Omar’s staffers out of the house.
Asked by Fox News Digital whether Omar had left the country amid rumours following the raid, Mynett expressed frustration with reporters and said their presence was disturbing neighbours.
“You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man,” he said.
The developments come amid an investigation by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) into Omar’s immigration paperwork. Federal agents searched her home on Monday, reportedly seizing her cellphone and passport, along with other items, according to US media reports.
The investigation is examining questions surrounding Omar’s age at the time her family arrived in the US and the circumstances under which she obtained citizenship. 
The precise scope of the criminal investigation has not been publicly established.
Mynett has maintained that he has no concerns about the investigation. Speaking to Fox News Digital earlier this week, he said Omar came to the US as a child refugee.
“My wife came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee,” Mynett said. “No concerns.”
Omar's relatives reportedly subpoenaed
The investigation has also reportedly extended to Omar’s relatives, with at least two family members receiving subpoenas, according to Fox News Digital. One of them was identified in reports as her sister, Sahra Noor.
Omar, who was born in Somalia, arrived in the US in 1995 with her family after fleeing the country’s conflict. She became a naturalised US citizen in 2000.
Questions have been raised about whether her age was accurately recorded in immigration documents. Reports have also highlighted a change to her birth year in records maintained by the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, from 1981 to 1982.
The allegations have drawn renewed scrutiny from Republicans, including President Donald Trump, who has previously questioned Omar’s citizenship and accused her of wrongdoing. Omar has rejected the allegations and described the investigations as politically motivated.
Financial disclosures under scrutiny
Separately, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has confirmed that her office is investigating Omar’s financial disclosures, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding the congresswoman.
The issue gained attention after Omar’s 2024 congressional financial disclosure listed business interests associated with Mynett, including a winery and a venture capital advisory firm, with a combined reported value running into millions of dollars.
Omar’s office subsequently amended the filing, saying the original disclosure had mistakenly reflected the total equity of the businesses rather than Mynett’s individual ownership interests. It also said the initial figures did not account for liabilities.
In the amended records, Mynett’s ownership interests in both businesses were listed at zero dollars, according to reports.
Trump questioned the discrepancy in a social media post on Tuesday, asking how Omar’s reported net worth could have reached as high as USD 30 million before being revised substantially downward.
Officials have indicated that the inquiry into Omar’s financial disclosures is separate from the search of her residence. Omar has denied wrongdoing in connection with the allegations.

articles.title: 'We'll knock it out fast': Trump says may target Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'We'll knock it out fast': Trump says may target Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility  The Times of IndiaExclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say  CNNTrump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters  Al JazeeraTrump says US may need to strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain  ReutersU.S. considers hitting Iran with 'Mother of All Bombs': report  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday said Washington may strike Iran's Pickaxe mountain facility as he seeks to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, while ruling out the use of nuclear weapons in the ongoing war.
Speaking to Newsmax, Trump said the US was examining the possibility of targeting the site, which is buried deep underground near one of Iran's alleged main nuclear facilities, Reuters reported.
"Their nuclear is buried under millions of tons of mountain. Now we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there,” Trump said.
“We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast," he added.
Trump also rejected the need to deploy nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the US could achieve its objectives without them.
"I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to," Trump told the news outlet.
Trump said the US wanted to ensure the nuclear weapons never fall into Iranian hands "because if they had it, they would use it."
He reiterated that he was not considering sending American ground troops into the country.
The war began in February with US-Israeli strikes against Iran.
Trump did not clarify whether he had authorised the use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “mother of all bombs”, against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
However, he stressed that the MOAB was not a nuclear weapon.
According to Anadolu Agency, Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain lies around 1.5 kilometres south of the Natanz nuclear facility and is believed to house nuclear centrifuges relocated from other sites. The mountain is made of solid granite and extends to a depth of up to 600 metres, with Iran allegedly excavating more than 100 metres beneath it.
There have also been unverified claims that some of Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium may be stored at the site, where it could be further enriched for potential use in nuclear weapons.
Earlier, Iran foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said “no nuclear activity is taking place” at Pickaxe Mountain, dismissing US threats as “a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage”.

articles.title: Catch a bully by its horns: How India can turn the latest round of US visa curbs affecting Indian techies - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Catch a bully by its horns: How India can turn the latest round of US visa curbs affecting Indian techies  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Import people or export work' was a stark fact conveyed by Nasscom to a top US official and several Congressmen at the time of the first 'outsourcing backlash' in the early 2000s. It reached a crescendo in 2003-04 and was an important issue in that year's US presidential election campaigning.
It did end soon after polls, as more people understood the win-win India-US IT relationship. Consequently - despite continuing battles - things on the visa front did become easier for Indian IT companies. The vast improvement in political ties post-2004, too, helped.
Now, there is a new reality, with India-US ties sinking lower by the day, more precipitously after Operation Sindoor last year. A few days back, the US added one more irritant that could further worsen overall ties. It not only made allegations against eminent Indian IT companies but also disallowed them from PERM (Permanent Labour Certification Programme). J D Vance even added some nasty words about Indian IT workers in the US.
PERM enables employers to apply to move their H-1B employees to a more permanent visa. For many, and for long, this was their dream path, possibly leading to a 'green card', even US citizenship. At the company level, the US allegations pose reputational challenges, especially given their standing as well-governed organisations. But work-wise, closing of this visa will hardly affect them. One commentator estimates that last year, only 1,400 applications, of a total of almost 1.2 lakh, for PERM were from Indian IT companies.
The overall impact on the industry and country will be, at best, marginal. But for individuals who may have taken loans or mortgages in the expectation of a long-term/permanent visa-enabling future dollar-earnings stream, this will be a major jolt. Most will now have to return to India.
This will also affect the many others who looked at this as a possible future path. Already, other visa restrictions - on post-education work visas through the OPT (optional practical training) window - are leading to more Indian students returning, some with degrees from top US institutions. Those already working there are now worried about visa extensions and long-term prospects.
For India, this returning stream presents extraordinary opportunities. At a time when emerging technologies like AI, quantum, genetics and space require high-order talent, 'brain gain' from returnees provides a quick-fix solution, even as we, hopefully, undertake major educational reforms to upgrade the terrible state of our education infrastructure and system. For this opportunity, we must thank the US.
The $315 bn industry is vital for India. It employs 6 mn directly, and ~10 mn indirectly. It's also India's biggest forex earner. The US accounts for $150 bn of the industry's $250 bn exports. While remote delivery and AI have advanced, we still need to send people to deliver services. Given this, it may not be unintentional that Indian IT is in the crosshairs of the Trump regime. We need our own leverage.
For this, at the broader level of overall India-US ties, we could take 4 key steps:
The US has, as part of its sanctions, threatened to impose penal tariffs on Indian exports if we continue to buy Russian oil (never mind that US will now import Russian diesel). So far, India has, at least in formal statements, resisted this, though it seems to have cut back on Russian oil imports. In retaliation, India could impose sanctions - limited to specific companies - on those exporting arms to Pakistan, a declared enemy.
Air travel in and from India is seeing a boom. As a result, hundreds of new aircraft will be ordered in the next few years. We could ensure, through appropriate formal or informal means, that the orders are placed with Airbus and other non-US companies.
Almost any military equipment can now be sourced from two or more countries. Today, India is a large, growing and attractive market for foreign suppliers, despite increasing indigenisation. For whatever is being procured from abroad, we could ensure that US companies are not among our suppliers.
In any case, US equipment is generally the most expensive and unreliable in terms of future supplies of spares and upgrades. The same is true of nuclear power plants where it will be wise to stay away from US equipment.
Negotiations on the Indo-US trade deal must include a proviso for free movement of people for delivering of contracted services. This is distinct from immigration or long-term visas.
None of this needs to be actually done. But these are weapons in our armoury, which the US must be made aware of, to be used selectively, if and when appropriate. Of course, their efficacy depends on 3 things that will give us leverage:
A strong indigenous tech base.
Good relations with alternative suppliers, including Europe, Japan, South Korea and Russia.
A non-antagonistic - if not cooperative - relationship with China.
It is well known that placating a bully never works. The demands keep escalating. Standing up often makes the bully behave better. We have recent evidence of this in concrete terms: procurement of S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems from Russia - that played a crucial role in Operation Sindoor - which the US was pressurising us to cancel, and the continuing import of Russian oil. Our refusal to back down in both cases led to a US back off.
Finally, if all else fails, we can play the trump card of offering the expertise and know-how of our Election Commission to ensure a Trump victory in the US mid-term elections next month.
Synopsis
Visa restrictions imposed by the US on Indian IT companies may impact individuals working on temporary visas. Many Indian workers may now have to return to India due to these restrictions. Despite these challenges, returnees present opportunities for India in emerging technologies and industries. Additionally, India's relationship with the US requires strategic actions to maintain balance in trade and diplomacy.

articles.title: Urban Indian households likely to spend nearly INR 20,000 on average this festive season; 6% lower than 2025 - Loktej English
articles.summary: Urban Indian households likely to spend nearly INR 20,000 on average this festive season; 6% lower than 2025  Loktej English
articles.full_text:
New Delhi [India], October 14: With Navratri, Dussehra and Diwali approaching, India’s festive season, traditionally the biggest window for discretionary purchases, is opening against a tightening economic backdrop. Retail inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), rose to 5.54% in September 2026 from 4.83% in August, its eleventh consecutive monthly increase, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) on October 12. Food inflation surged to 7.74% from 5.97%, with onion prices more than doubling year-on-year, and a home-cooked vegetarian thali cost about 10% more than a year earlier. On October 7, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, its first hike in over three and a half years, and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening. Governor Sanjay Malhotra said rate cuts are off the table in the near term. The RBI raised its FY27 CPI inflation projection to 5.2% from 5.0%, and expects inflation to peak at 6.0% in the October-December quarter, which coincides with the festive season.
• In total, 57% urban Indian households surveyed likely to spend this festive season.
• 34% of households spending likely to fund a significant part (25% or more) of festive spending from Savings.
• 72% of households spending likely to buy clothing/fashion products; 45% also buying appliances.
• 9% households likely to spend over INR 1 lakh this festive season; 30% between INR 10,000 and 1 lakh.
The RBI has flagged that price pressures are becoming broad-based, with 37% of items in the CPI basket rising more than 4% by August, and that cyclical inflation risks are no longer benign given elevated oil prices, tighter global conditions and a deficient monsoon. Brent crude was trading at about USD 101 per barrel on October 6, over 50% higher than a year ago, and wholesale inflation, as measured by the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), jumped to 11.39% in September from 9.92% in August on higher fuel and manufacturing costs, according to government data released on October 14. The hike will also make festive borrowing costlier: if passed on in full, the EMI on an INR 50 lakh, 25-year home loan rises by about INR 817 a month.
While the RBI raised its FY27 GDP growth projection to 7.1% from 6.7%, citing resilient private consumption, its household surveys point to growing caution. In the July 2026 round of the Urban Consumer Confidence Survey, the Current Situation Index fell to 88.3 from 90.7 and the Future Expectations Index to 115.3 from 118.7. The net response on current spending on non-essential items stood at just 3.3, against 86.7 for essential items, while the employment net response fell to -21.9 from -14.4. Households also expect prices to rise 9.4% over the next year, according to the RBI’s Inflation Expectations Survey of Households. These expectations carry weight: RBI working papers by Purnima Shaw and RK Sinha find that since the pandemic, household inflation forecasts have been more accurate than professional forecasts about 65% of the time, against 39% for professional forecasts.
Household balance sheets are also under strain. While net household financial savings improved to 7% of Gross National Disposable Income (GNDI) in FY25 from 5.8% in FY24, largely due to lower borrowings, an Economic and Political Weekly analysis published in early September notes that household financial liabilities reached 45.8% of GDP by March 2026, having grown faster than financial assets since mid-2022. New fixed deposits offered 5.67% in August, below the 9.4% inflation households expect, implying negative real returns, yet the share of term deposits in total bank deposits rose from about 55% to nearly 62% between March 2022 and March 2026.
Early festive indicators point to spending that is selective. Gross GST collections rose 14.7% year-on year to INR 2.04 lakh crore in September 2026, though domestic GST grew a more modest 10.1%. Vehicle retail sales hit a record 25.37 lakh units in September, up 31.8% year-on-year, though the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) cautioned that growth was flattered by a low base, as buyers had deferred purchases ahead of GST 2.0 in September 2025.
Online festive sales, which opened with Amazon’s Great Indian Festival on October 8 and Flipkart’s Big Billion Days on October 9, show a similar split. Platforms have reported strong traffic, with Flipkart recording 6.3 million concurrent users and about 60% of demand from non-metro customers, and Meesho reporting a 75% year-onyear rise in Day 1 orders across fashion, beauty and festive décor. Big-ticket electronics, however, are under pressure: Counterpoint Research expects festive smartphone volumes to fall 12% year-on-year as rising memory chip costs push up device prices, even as market value rises 5%. Unlike last year, when GST rate cuts effective September 22, 2025 coincided with the start of major sales, there is no tax-led tailwind this season.
Against this backdrop, LocalCircles conducted its Mood of the Consumer survey to understand how much urban Indian households plan to spend this festive season, what they intend to buy and how they plan to fund it. The survey received over 67,000 responses from urban household consumers located across 307 districts of India.
The survey indicates that urban Indian households are likely to spend INR 20,000 on average on discretionary purchases this festive season. Based on the spending levels indicated in the survey, LocalCircles estimates total urban household festive spending at INR 1.97 lakh crore in 2026, 6% lower than INR 2.10 lakh crore in 2025. This reverses last year’s rise from INR 1.85 lakh crore in 2024, a year in which the GST rate cuts effective September 22, 2025 coincided with the start of the festive season. While 57% of households surveyed are likely to spend this festive season, 31% plan no discretionary spending at all. Of those spending, 72% will buy clothing/fashion products, and 83% will dip into savings to some extent, including 34% who will fund 25% or more of their festive spending from savings. In response, 31% said no discretionary spending is planned, while 18% expect to spend less than INR 10,000 and 15% between INR 10,001 and INR 25,000. Another 9% expect to spend INR 25,001-50,000, 6% INR 50,001-1 lakh and 9% INR 1-10 lakh, while 12% could not say.
In aggregate, 57% of urban households surveyed are likely to spend this festive season. 30% expect to spend between INR 10,000 and INR 1 lakh and 9% over INR 1 lakh, while 18% will keep their festive budget below INR 10,000. 'Real Boss of India': US Secretary of State to Skip New Delhi for Jamnagar, Mumbai
New Delhi: For the first time, a US secretary of state is set to visit India without any planned meetings in New Delhi.
Marco Rubio’s itinerary instead includes Mumbai and Jamnagar during his trip from October 17–22 to India and Uzbekistan. In Uzbekistan, he will visit Samarkand, the second-largest city of the country and notably, also not the capital.
Although it is Ahmedabad that has emerged as the centre-stage of India’s diplomatic engagements ever since Narendra Modi’s prime ministership began in 2014 – Modi has hosted Trump, Xi Jinping, Shinzo Abe and Benjamin Netanyahu there – this is the first time Jamnagar has been thrust into the spotlight.
Jamnagar is home to the Indian oligarch Mukesh Ambani family’s major business interests where Rubio will meet “senior government officials”. It has the Reliance Industries’ refinery, which is the world’s largest single-site complex. In March, US President Donald Trump had announced the construction of a $300-billion refinery on the southern US border backed by Reliance Industries.
Meanwhile, legislation in waiting in the US could impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing Russian oil, including India. The US-India bilateral trade deal also hangs fire.
This visit comes as US oligarch Elon Musk described Ambani as the “real boss of India” last week.
While the White House has announced Rubio’s itinerary October 13, the exact date of his arrival in India is yet to be confirmed.
“Several issues of a bilateral nature will be discussed,” said Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said a day ago on October 14, when he was questioned on the agenda of Rubio’s visit.
Rubio's May visit to India had included a highly publicised visit to the Missionaries of Charity headquarters in Kolkata, which in turn thrust the stringent Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) back into the spotlight.

articles.summary: Yemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport  Al JazeeraStrikes hit Yemen's Aden airport; Saudi-led coalition intercepts drones, missiles  CGTNYemen's Government-Controlled City Of Aden Attacked In Houthi Strikes  NDTVAt least two killed in explosions near palace in Aden used by Yemen's govt. in latest Houthi attack  The HinduHouthi missiles strike Yemen presidential palace, killing five  The Guardian

Yemen’s internationally recognised government says the Houthis have launched missiles at the airport in Aden, a day after carrying out a deadly attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city.
Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said two missiles landed near the runway at Aden International Airport on Friday, 500 metres (1,640 feet) from an aircraft that was preparing to take off.
All passengers and crew were safe, he said on X, thanking “divine providence” for preventing a potential “horrific humanitarian catastrophe” and calling the attacks on the airport “a grave violation of international laws and norms”.
The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said on Friday that they launched an attack on “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province” as well as a weapons depot, the AFP news agency reported.
The latest attack in Aden, which is the seat of the internationally recognised government, comes amid continued heavy fighting in Yemen’s reignited civil war between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Yemeni government forces said earlier on Friday that troops had advanced in Marib province northeast of Sanaa.
Military spokesman Majed al-Nazili said Yemeni government forces, with air support, had made significant “territorial gains” in the eastern part of the province, securing “key positions”.
He also said Yemeni forces had “neutralised” more than 430 Houthi fighters in 24 hours, while destroying or disabling more than 100 of their vehicles and military assets.
Elsewhere, in Taiz governorate, which has emerged as a key battlefront in the war, Yemeni government forces claimed to have fended off several “large-scale” Houthi attacks, inflicting “heavy losses” on the group.
Yemeni government forces also claimed to have captured a specialised drone team affiliated with the Houthis in the Taiz area.
In recent weeks, Houthi forces have encircled the city of Taiz — Yemen’s third largest urban centre — by cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis.
Missiles over Riyadh
Elsewhere on Friday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had downed missiles and drones over Riyadh and other parts of Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging Houthi attacks against the kingdom, including by arming and training the group.
But Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday rejected the accusation, saying Tehran had not played a role in any Houthi operations. The ministry also reiterated a proposal to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh.
The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the government to flee.
An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides.
A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in July.
In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the Red Sea port city.
The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.

articles.title: India-US Ties: Beyond the turbulence - Deccan Herald
articles.summary: India-US Ties: Beyond the turbulence  Deccan Herald
articles.full_text:
India’s policy of engaging America, managing China, cultivating Europe, reassuring Russia and partnering with Japan is an expression of its strategic autonomy. But its relationship with the United States is undoubtedly the most critical. The visit of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will skip New Delhi but travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar, will test India’s multi-alignment in a multipolar world. It will also demonstrate the growing role of corporate interests in bilateral relations.
Disquiet in bilateral ties
Contrary to the positive trajectory of the India-US partnership over the past three and a half decades, the relationship is now under strain. Washington’s desire for a formal alliance or a defence framework entailing mutual security obligations contrasts with India’s approach of engaging the US as a key strategic partner while pursuing multi-alignment.
Recently, economic ties have come under strain because of unilateral tariffs, stalled negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement, the threat of secondary sanctions linked to India’s imports of Russian oil and its engagement with Iran, and restrictions on the mobility of Indian professionals through H-1B visas. On the political front, there has been disquiet over Washington’s embrace of Pakistan and the prospect of a G2 understanding with China. A reset in India-US relations, based on mutually beneficial outcomes and sensitivity to each other’s core interests and concerns rather than a merely transactional approach, is urgently needed.
The America First moment
Amid the rise of emerging global powers such as India and China, as well as middle powers, the US has sought to maintain its dominant position through domestic rejuvenation while realigning external relations, rewriting treaties and reviewing global commitments. This has placed a greater burden of responsibility on allies, particularly those in the transatlantic alliance and the Far East, to share costs, invest in the US and plan for higher defence budgets. As strategic partners, India and the US have also entered a turbulent phase marked by uncertainty, but their strategic engagement has endured.
The current unease is not a passing phase. It is likely to continue as the US undertakes structural adjustments to deal with an assertive China, with implications for allies and partners as well. A study of US perceptions and the narratives shaping its current approaches and policies would benefit its partners.
Understanding the US mindset
US policymakers have often claimed that India’s policy of non-alignment and strategic autonomy limits the scope for an alliance. In contrast, Pakistan was a more willing ally, despite its deep ties with China, and became a recipient of defence assistance, while the US turned a blind eye even to its sponsorship of terrorism. Yet the project of drawing India into an alliance did not die. In fact, areas of convergence in the India-US strategic partnership extended to maritime security in the Indo-Pacific, the supply of high-tech military hardware, sensitive defence agreements, and cooperation in critical materials and nuclear energy, although the relationship was not a security alliance.
The Rubio visit could serve as a fulcrum for deepening cooperation in advanced technologies, defence, critical materials, resilient supply chains and corporate engagement. Discussions aimed at injecting realism into US-Pakistan relations, improving understanding of a multipolar Asia, intensifying engagement in the Quad and reviving the Indo-Pacific agenda will be crucial.
Rapid growth in bilateral trade had prompted the setting of an ambitious target of $500 billion, but the pace has slowed and India’s trade surplus shrank last year. India faced high tariffs that reduced its competitiveness and increased uncertainty. The India-US trade agreement remained stalled amid US demands for market access in areas such as sensitive agriculture and dairy sectors, intellectual property rights (IPR), the data economy and others.
There is a perception in the US that India’s reforms have not lived up to expectations. US corporates have complained of regulatory impediments that restrict the ease of doing business and hamper greater flows of trade, investment and technology. Domestic sentiment in the US has conflated these concerns with the migration of Indian professionals to the country. These perceptions have negatively affected economic engagement and migration. There is thus an urgent need to conclude the trade deal to restore confidence and promote the expansion of trade, investment, technology, mobility, skills cooperation, global value chains and supply chains. At a time when new rules are being framed for the digital economy and advanced technology, cooperation between India and the US can offer mutually beneficial options.
Energy security has emerged as a priority in both economic and political terms. The wars in Ukraine and West Asia, the weaponisation of maritime chokepoints and disruptions to energy security have weakened global economic growth. The recent US decision to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel shipments provides a breather. Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar assumes relevance in this context. Moreover, peace and stability in West Asia are needed to stabilise energy markets and cool prices. Greater stability would help reduce inflation, increase employment and revive growth and globalisation.
The Trump administration’s unilateral approach has further weakened the multilateral, rules-based order. There is growing support for reform of the multilateral system, although its contours are still emerging. There is also concern about China’s hegemonic power. This may be the time to explore networks of plurilateral initiatives in which India and the US are partners, such as the G20, G7 Outreach, I2U2, the Quad, IPEF and IMEC, as steps towards reformed global governance.
The India-US relationship is in a turbulent phase, but the strategic engagement remains stable. Both countries need to pay attention to the relationship, demonstrate sensitivity to each other’s core interests and concerns, and pursue future-oriented, mutually beneficial outcomes. The pursuit of domestic economic growth through reforms, coupled with principled yet flexible diplomacy with the US, will transform India into a global power that would be difficult to ignore. India must engage a wider community of policymakers, business leaders and new stakeholders in the US to strengthen its bench strength and advocacy. Finally, this is not a zero-sum game: the simultaneous growth of India and the US poses no threat to either country but instead offers better opportunities to their citizens and to humankind.
(The writer is a former diplomat and currently a professor at Jindal Global University)

TOI correspondent from London: Indian national Deepak Sandhu, who came to the UK on a student visa, was on Friday sent to jail for life with a minimum of 28 years for murdering a Chinese woman he met at a brothel.
It took a jury at the Old Bailey just two hours to convict Sandhu (24) of murdering Chinese national Xiaoqing Ke (39), who he met at a brothel in Southampton where he was a customer and she was working. He was also convicted of perverting the course of justice. Sandhu denied the charges. He sat in the dock with a Punjabi interpreter.
The court heard that Sandhu had a brief relationship with Xiaoqing, a single mother-of-two, during which he fabricated an identity of being a model and actor. The pair communicated using the Google Translate app.
Sandhu had entered the UK in Sep 2024. He was thrown off his IT course at Southampton Solent University and his visa was revoked six months later for poor attendance; he was actually working as a casual labourer on building sites.
After Xiaoqing discovered that Sandhu had been lying and had stolen £500 from her handbag, she ended the relationship in Aug 2025.
Sandhu pestered Xiaoqing and persuaded her to meet by promising to repay her money. 
In reality he wanted revenge, the court was told.
Doorbell camera footage from Xiaoqing’s Airbnb captured him arriving with his face wrapped in a scarf and leaving after about 90 minutes. Police discovered her body the following day. A post-mortem confirmed that she died as a result of stab wounds.
Sandhu booked a one-way flight from Birmingham to Mumbai but was arrested by police travelling on a coach from Southampton to Birmingham Airport on Dec 12.

India’s massive youth population is a key element of the recent unrest sweeping the country. However, the more immediate problem is the growing gap between aspirations and access to secure employment. In 2026, unemployment was estimated at nearly 18 percent among urban youth and roughly 24-27 percent among young urban women, though sources and definitions of statistical figures in India often vary. The pressure this gap foments helps explain how a medical school entrance exam became a national flashpoint: On May 3, more than 2.2 million candidates reportedly sat the NEET, one of many competitive exams that serve as major pathways to professional education and stable work.
When Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant compared in open court young people without jobs or professions to “cockroaches,” a new protest movement was born. Kant later said he was referring to people who obtain fraudulent degrees rather than youth as a whole, but frustration over his comment and the state of employment in India led to the establishment of the satirically named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The protests that followed initially focused on educational grievances but later turned into a broader campaign against the Election Commission’s revisions to voter lists, which reportedly led to the removal of approximately 130 million voter names since 2025. The commission maintains that the changes are intended to remove deceased, duplicate and otherwise ineligible entries, while opposition leaders allege that eligible voters have been wrongly excluded and dispute the process’ political neutrality. Authorities responded to the CJP-led Oct. 10 mobilization with mass detentions and restrictions on demonstrations. Whatever happens to the movement, persistent difficulties in securing employment and translating educational success into economic opportunity could sustain the underlying grievances, even if the CJP itself loses momentum.

New Delhi [India], October 16 (ANI): National highway projects awarded in India increased by 62.9 per cent year-on-year to 2,236.3 kilometres during April-September of the current financial year, indicating a stronger pipeline of road construction projects, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) on Friday.
The rise in project awards indicates a stronger pipeline of highway construction work, which could support infrastructure development and create opportunities for construction companies in the coming months.
Highlighting the increase, the ministry said in its quarterly infrastructure performance update, 'Road Transport and Highways sector recorded 2,236.3 km of National Highway projects awarded in FY 2026-27 [April-September] registering a robust 62.9% YoY growth.'
The ministry added, 'This significant increase strengthens the pipeline of highway infrastructure development, paving the way for enhanced connectivity, improved logistics efficiency, and sustained economic growth.'
The figures reflect new highway projects awarded during the first six months of FY27 and not the actual length of roads constructed or completed during the period.
The latest data also showed growth in electronic toll collection activity across the national highway network.
Electronic toll collection transactions increased 24.1 per cent year-on-year to 225.2 crore during April-September FY27, while the total value of toll collections rose 11.7 per cent to Rs 36,994.5 crore.
According to the ministry, the figures indicate 'sustained adoption of electronic tolling and increasing digitalization of toll collection across the road network.'
The figures were released as part of the quarterly update of the PAIMANA (Project Assessment, Infrastructure Monitoring & Analytics for Nation-building) Performance Dashboard, launched by MoSPI in April 2026.
The dashboard monitors infrastructure performance across six sectors, including roads, railways, power, civil aviation, telecommunications, and ports and waterways.
The latest update has expanded the dashboard to 184 indicators, with the addition of 21 new indicators to strengthen infrastructure monitoring and policymaking. (ANI)

As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to India, the U.S.-India relationship appears to many to be facing another cycle of volatility. Trade negotiations have plateaued, disagreements over Russia have intensified, public criticisms have sharpened, and public opinion of the United States has hit a record low in India. Washington’s weaponization of trade and its handling of regional crises have revived doubts about American reliability, while New Delhi’s intransigence on a trade deal, sustained embrace of Russia, and renewed engagement with China have revived India skepticism for some in Washington.
However, beneath the public disputes, the two countries continue to deepen functional cooperation on defense-industrial relations, space, AI infrastructure, and maritime operational security. Despite the downturn, the partnership retains the ability to work together on critically important issues.
This contradiction may have a simple explanation. Failures are public, politically salient, and often immediately apparent, but successes are often hidden from view, highly technical, or take years to materialize. Consequently, perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.
Real Turbulence
This period of turbulence largely began over trade, and the two governments remain divided over market access, tariffs, and India’s purchases of Russian oil. These economic disputes reflect a deeper geopolitical divergence: Washington (and Brussels) increasingly regard Moscow as an active threat to the European security order, and the latest round of U.S. sanctions legislation has caught New Delhi in the crossfire. In contrast, India views Russia through the lenses of energy security, legacy arms dependence, and strategic flexibility, and it bristles at the West’s censure, which it sees as hypocritical.
Significant shifts in U.S. legal immigration policy have also stressed the relationship. The crackdown by President Donald Trump’s administration on Indian technology firms days before a White House delegation travels to New Delhi to revive technology partnerships—under the TRUST Initiative—raises questions of policy coherence.
The past year of U.S. foreign policy has also strained the relationship. Indian officials have criticized renewed U.S. engagement with Pakistan as lacking empathy for India’s counterterrorism challenges, and the war with Iran has created severe economic pressures on India, forcing New Delhi to revert to higher levels of Russian oil imports. Furthermore, the United States’ courtship of China has revived Indian fears of a so-called G2 bipolar world that could constrain India’s rise.
Such disagreements affect public expectations about how each country might behave in a future crisis. Once confidence begins to decline, every dispute risks becoming evidence of a larger betrayal.
Quiet, Banal, Strategic Progress
Focusing on politically salient tensions obscures the steady, often overlooked advances that constitute a major strategic upgrade for the two sides.
Despite the sound and fury of new tariffs, U.S.-India trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to a new peak of nearly $240 billion, with the United States remaining India’s top export destination.
Technology cooperation has also been quietly growing. Take the NISAR satellite, which collects data on changes in Earth’s land, ice, water, and vegetation. Its launch in 2025 was the culmination of a decade of collaboration between two complex bureaucracies—NASA and the ISRO—that successfully overcame regulatory hurdles and political transitions to deploy cutting-edge radars to space.
Another example is AI. Major U.S. technology companies pledged nearly $68 billion in AI infrastructure investments in India last year. The opening of semiconductor corporation Micron’s first assembly and test facility in India on February 28 served as a landmark fulfillment of a 2023 commitment, but it was drowned out by the launch of U.S. Operation Epic Fury against Iran. A few weeks ago, Applied Materials and Lam Research announced their own investments in India’s semiconductor ecosystem.
The defense relationship has proved especially durable. This year, the United States and India are on pace for a record number of joint exercises, including one that involved multiple days of combined air assault operations and Indian and U.S. troops working together at a uniquely granular level just 30 miles from the India-China border. The new ten-year framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership calls for closer coordination across advanced domains, expanded information-sharing, more complex exercises, and deeper defense-industrial ties.
The maritime dimension is particularly consequential. For all the hand-wringing in Washington about the Indian Army’s dependence on Russian arms, the Indian Navy has acquired an array of interoperable U.S. platforms for maritime reconnaissance: P-8 maritime patrol aircraft, MH-60R anti-submarine warfare helicopters, and MQ-9B high-altitude, long-endurance surveillance drones. All are designed to enhance India’s burden-sharing in the Indian Ocean while complementing U.S. naval strategy in the broader Indo-Pacific—including a new Quad initiative for Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration. Behind closed doors, Indian officials routinely talk about joint tracking of Chinese submarines. There is also far too little appreciation of India’s growing role in the U.S.-led Combined Maritime Forces—the first time India has joined a military coalitional effort outside the UN framework.
Hidden Signals
Some of the most consequential achievements—especially in India’s advanced undersea and space domains—remain invisible amid the din of political disputes. For instance, American capital, technology, labs, and accelerators have supported India’s space, semiconductor, and digital ecosystems. However, these connections remain confined to private relationships between firms and, even when publicized, are rarely presented as broader evidence of strategic interdependence.
In other instances, cooperation is deliberately concealed. During India’s 2020 border crisis with China, Washington played a significant role in expediting equipment, gear for extreme cold weather, and intelligence support, but India requested that this all be kept quiet. Beyond indirect assistance, when India leased contractor-owned, contractor-operated MQ-9B Predator drones to surveil its maritime approaches and border with China, it likely relied on former U.S. military pilots to operate those drones on behalf of the Indian Navy from an Indian military base. A couple of years later, U.S. intelligence support likely helped the Indian Army interdict a Chinese army gray-zone probe, but this was never acknowledged.
These episodes suggest Washington can be reliable in a serious security crisis, but that information has gone largely unobserved by the Indian public and many within the Indian government. Indian leadership has concealed these facts to manage escalation, and Washington has respected New Delhi’s preference for discretion, even though the secrecy meant a missed opportunity to deepen trust.
The United States is also guilty of passing up opportunities to spotlight strategic breakthroughs. For example, the full details of the 2025 U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership framework have yet to be made public. This secrecy has consequences: Investors hold back on big bets, export controllers act with excess caution, and lawmakers discount the trade-offs when they choose to enact sanctions, solidifying a strategic ceiling for the relationship.
Delayed Results
Long delays between commitments and delivery compound the visibility problem. Political leaders seek clear results on marquee defense or technology projects within an electoral term, while bureaucracies may take years to turn announcements into contracts and capabilities.
Some of this is the normal lag that occurs when two governments reconcile different acquisition systems, export controls, and technology expectations. India took four years to implement the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness after its announcement in 2022. Some of the MQ-9B Predator drones cleared for sale in 2017 during Trump’s first administration were not contracted until the end of former president Joe Biden’s administration and will be delivered to India around the time the next U.S. administration takes office in 2029. Such lags are hardly unique to the U.S.-India relationship: India’s BrahMos missile joint venture with Russia took more than ten years from initial agreement to induction of the missile, and nearly thirty years later, India has still not fully indigenized the missile.
These delays are also partially the fault of the rigid Indian defense acquisition process. The recently announced Javelin anti-tank guided missile purchase and co-production memorandum of understanding come after more than a decade of on-again, off-again discussions constrained by export controls. articles.summary: Dark clouds in the economic silver lining  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
India’s growth prospects have brightened just as the world economy is becoming a more expensive place in which to borrow. This month, the IMF has raised its growth forecast for India to 7 percent, while the World Bank and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development put it at 7.1 percent this financial year. These assessments recognise the economy’s resilience. But rising prices and interest rates will test how widely, and how durably, that growth translates into prosperity.
Across the US, Britain and Japan, governments are paying more to borrow for the long term. The IMF reports that the average interest rate on 10-year government bonds across the G7 rose by more than one percentage point between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades. These movements may seem remote from an Indian household’s concerns. Their consequences will arrive through loan repayments, employment, prices and government budgets.
Several forces are at work. Expensive energy is reviving inflation. Governments need money for defence, ageing populations, infrastructure and existing obligations. Meanwhile, enormous investments in artificial intelligence are competing for finance. Lenders are demanding greater compensation for committing their money for years, particularly when inflation and public debt make future returns less certain.
Japan adds another complication. For years, exceptionally low Japanese interest rates encouraged investors to borrow in yen and invest elsewhere, including in emerging markets. As Japanese borrowing costs rise, this strategy becomes less attractive. A strengthening yen can also make repayment more expensive. Positions built gradually can be reversed abruptly, transmitting selling pressure across countries whose underlying economic conditions may have changed little.
The AI boom is encountering its own financing test. Building data centres requires vast spending on chips, electricity, cooling and land, often well before revenues arrive. The largest technology companies have substantial earnings, but borrowing has become increasingly important across the expanding network of infrastructure providers and newer firms. Higher interest charges make uncertain future profits harder to justify.
The sharp sell-offs in South Korean technology shares this week show how quickly enthusiasm can turn into anxiety. There are fears of an AI investment bubble. The crash this week does not establish that AI’s economic promise has evaporated. They do reveal growing doubts about investment commitments and the debt supporting them. A technology can transform productivity while some of the businesses financing its expansion suffer heavy losses.
Governments face a related problem on a much larger scale. They must finance current deficits and replace loans that mature. As older, cheaper debt is replaced with more expensive borrowing, interest bills rise. Unless revenues keep pace, further borrowing follows. Global bond markets are facing intense competition for costlier funds and are feeling the squeeze from debt repayments.
India has important strengths. Its government borrows predominantly in rupees; and domestic banks, insurers and retirement funds provide a substantial investor base. This reduces dependence on foreign creditors. It also means that government borrowing draws heavily on savings held on behalf of Indian households. A dependable domestic funding base cushions external shocks. But it cannot eliminate the cost of borrowing.
The Union budget makes the vulnerability plain. Interest payments this year are estimated at approximately ₹14 lakh crore. That is nearly ₹49 out of every ₹100 of tax revenue retained by the Centre after sharing with states. Even including non-tax income, interest absorbs about 40 percent of revenue receipts. By comparison, the average for all low- to middle-income countries is 11-15 percent. India’s debt service costs are remarkably high for a country with enormous development needs. State governments face their own repayment obligations.
A rise in interest rates does not immediately reprice every government loan. Most existing bonds continue paying their contracted interest. The pressure accumulates through fresh borrowing and refinancing, gradually reducing room for schools, hospitals, infrastructure and support for vulnerable households. Strong economic growth helps by expanding revenues, but spending commitments can grow too.
India’s inflation picture has, meanwhile, changed considerably. September retail inflation reached 5.54 percent, while wholesale inflation accelerated to 11.39 percent from 9.92 percent in August, indicating substantial pressure on production costs. Businesses face rising costs even as households face higher living expenses. Companies must either absorb these costs through lower profits or pass them on to customers, risking weaker demand. The cost of expensive imported oil must still be absorbed somewhere: in oil company margins, government revenues and fiscal deficit, or eventual price increases. A weaker rupee compounds the burden.
The RBI has begun raising rates. It cannot produce more oil or repair a deficient monsoon. But it must prevent an initial supply shock from spreading into persistent inflation and weakening confidence in the currency. Higher rates abroad also make it harder to retain mobile foreign capital while keeping domestic borrowing unusually cheap.
Special measures such as the foreign currency scheme for non-residents can buy time. They cannot provide a permanent substitute for confidence and sustainable external financing. Borrowed dollars carry repayment obligations, while incentives and exchange-rate protection can impose costs. When incoming dollars are purchased by the RBI, rupee liquidity increases; absorbing it creates another policy challenge. Conversely, selling dollars to support the rupee withdraws rupees. The overall effect depends on the balance of these operations.
For households, rising prices and borrowing costs can reinforce each other. Food and fuel leave less money for other purchases. Floating-rate home loans can require higher monthly payments or longer repayment periods. Families already dependent on personal loans or revolving credit-card balances have less room to absorb setbacks. The household-debt-to-GDP ratio is at historic highs. Rising defaults are a risk to monitor, rather than grounds for declaring an inevitable banking crisis.
Nor does faster bank lending necessarily mean a new investment boom. Some companies may simply be replacing expensive bond finance with bank loans. Others need larger loans to pay higher input bills. Neither necessarily represents additional factories or jobs.
Private investment depends on expected demand, existing capacity, reliable infrastructure and predictable policy. Cheaper credit helps, especially smaller businesses, but cannot persuade a company to expand indefinitely when customers are reluctant to spend. Equally, allowing inflation to erode household purchasing power can undermine the demand on which investment depends.
There are beneficiaries of higher rates, too. Former RBI governor D Subbarao recalled meeting industrialists who always wanted lower rates. But pensioners who wanted higher ones were a silent constituency. Retirees living on deposits deserve consideration alongside borrowers. Their concern is whether interest income preserves purchasing power after inflation and tax.
India’s task is, therefore, to preserve growth while managing these competing pressures. Monetary policy needs support from credible government borrowing plans, measures to ease food and energy constraints, and targeted protection for vulnerable households. Keeping credit cheap at any cost would merely postpone the adjustment. Strong growth provides an opportunity to strengthen economic resilience before rising interest bills consume more of it.
Ajit Ranade | Economist and Senior Fellow at the Pune International Centre

Synopsis
YSRCP leader YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has changed his stance by supporting youth protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. This shift suggests potential political shifts and realignments ahead of upcoming elections. Reddy's aggressive position against the Election Commission also indicates an evolving political strategy and outreach to various political factions. Speculation about a possible alliance with the Congress-led INDIA bloc has emerged following his recent meetings.
Reddy's change in stance comes amid increased scrutiny of the disproportionate asset cases against him, with a CBI court deciding to conduct daily hearings in the Enforcement Directorate cases alongside the ongoing CBI proceedings. With his principal rival N Chandrababu Naidu's TDP firmly entrenched in NDA, Reddy appears to be exploring alternative political equations in Delhi.

People familiar with the matter indicated that Reddy recently met the Congress brass and that the meeting was arranged by Vishnu Reddy, adviser to Tamil Nadu CM Joseph Vijay. There has also been speculation about a meeting between Reddy and Congress general secretary KC Venugopal in Bengaluru, although neither side has officially confirmed it. YSRCP, however, has maintained that these were "rumours" spread by TDP to show the party was moving closer to the Opposition camp.
Reddy has also questioned ECI's functioning, while YSRCP has raised nine questions concerning the conduct of the 2024 Andhra Pradesh elections. These include alleged discrepancies in polling percentages, electronic voting machine battery readings, vote counts and delays in releasing electoral documents.
Another indication of the changing political equations came in September when Reddy met a CPI delegation and announced joint protests against government policies. The outreach to the Left, which is part of the INDIA bloc, assumes significance against the backdrop of YSRCP's earlier reluctance to associate with the Opposition alliance.
For much of the past decade, Reddy maintained a carefully calibrated relationship with BJP, supporting key legislation in Parliament without formally joining NDA. Even after losing power in Andhra Pradesh in 2024, YSRCP largely avoided a direct confrontation with the Centre.
However, with the TDP now occupying a crucial position in the NDA, that political arrangement appears increasingly difficult to sustain. articles.summary: Russia building 'security zone' in Ukraine that won't be part of future peace talks: Putin  The Times of IndiaUkraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares  The GuardianPutin says Russia is building non-negotiable 'security zone' in Ukraine along border  ReutersRussia's President Putin visits armed forces' command post amid Russia-Ukraine conflict  The Lufkin Daily NewsPutin says Russia’s borde...

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday said Moscow is building a buffer “security zone” inside Ukraine which won’t be a part of any future peace negotiations, describing the move as necessary to protect Russia’s border regions.
Putin made the remarks during a visit to a command post of Russia’s joint military task force. He linked the operation to Ukraine’s incursion into Russia’s western Kursk region in 2024-25, saying Russian forces had been directed to push Ukrainian troops out of Russian territory and extend the operation into neighbouring Ukrainian territory.
“The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments.
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the proposed security zone would cover a stretch of 660 km (410 miles), with Russian forces controlling 70 per cent of the area.
Putin was also quoted by the Kremlin as saying that Russia still needed to capture more of Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Reuters reported.
The latest remarks follow the Kremlin’s announcement in July that Russia was working to establish a buffer zone along the border.
“Given the aggressive nature of the Kyiv regime, in order to ensure the safety of our citizens, we will have to create a security zone, or buffer zone,” Peskov had told a Russian journalist, according to Anadolu Agency.
Peskov said the initiative was progressing steadily and pointed to advances made by Russian troops.
“It is being created, and it is being created systematically,” he said in remarks carried by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass, arguing that “significant results” had been achieved in terms of Russian troop advances.
He also maintained that Moscow would continue the operation until the zone reached the scale it considered necessary for its security.
The spokesperson had remarked that no one should doubt that the “buffer zone” would be created “to the extent necessary to ensure our security.”
