The accused, Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, was arrested by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
US immigration agencies have arrested Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari, an Indian citizen, for allegedly voting illegally in the 2024 US general election after making a false citizenship claim. Chaudhari has been charged with one count of false information in voting and one count of making a false claim of citizenship in order to register to vote. According to the US Department of Justice (DOJ), he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on each count if convicted.
“Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences, including criminal charges and deportation. Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration will never allow the votes of American citizens to be cancelled out by non-citizens illegally voting in our elections. Only American citizens should be electing American leaders,” said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
The Trump administration has made cracking down on cases of suspected electoral fraud a key policy focus. President Trump and his allies have consistently contested the legitimacy of the 2020 presidential election, which Trump lost to Joe Biden.
Trump has also claimed that a DHS review, state voter rolls and public records identified approximately 278,000 non-citizens registered to vote in federal elections. The White House has pushed Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require voters to provide proof of citizenship and photo identification to vote in federal elections.
However, these efforts have largely stalled. Legal experts have raised concerns that burdensome documentation requirements could lead to thousands of Americans, particularly minorities, losing their ability to vote.
Chaudhari signed voter signature certificate
According to the DOJ, Chaudhari signed a voter signature certificate in Minnesota on November 5, 2024, which required him to swear or affirm that he was a citizen of the United States. A federal grand jury returned an indictment against Chaudhari on September 10, allowing the federal case against him to proceed.
“The right to vote is a sacred privilege of American citizenship, and every lawful voter deserves an election system in which that right is protected. The Department will hold accountable those who knowingly make false claims of citizenship in order to vote. The integrity of our elections depends on ensuring that only eligible citizens cast ballots and that every lawful vote is counted,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division.

articles.full_text:
Geographic and analytical scope: China and India, their Himalayan security relationship, bilateral industrial interdependence, US–India strategic cooperation, the wider Indo-Pacific and the differentiated interests of the European Union, Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom. The assessment covers developments through 16 October 2026 and examines strategic pathways to 2031.
Executive Summary — Bottom Line Up Front
The China–India relationship has entered a phase of selective diplomatic stabilisation without strategic reconciliation. The meeting between President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on 12 September 2026 confirmed a bilateral commitment to improving relations, while leaving the boundary dispute, industrial asymmetries and regional security competition unresolved.
The principal strategic judgment is that Beijing and New Delhi increasingly recognise the economic and geopolitical costs of confrontation, but neither government has abandoned its long-term security objectives. China’s advantage lies partly in its position within India’s manufacturing supply chains; India’s leverage derives from its growing market, geopolitical relevance and ability to maintain relationships with competing international centres of power.
Five developments define the current strategic environment:
- 12 September 2026: Xi and Modi reaffirmed political engagement at the BRICS summit, with border stability, market access and structural trade imbalances remaining central issues.
- October 2024: The bilateral patrolling understanding concerning Depsang and Demchok established an important mechanism for reducing immediate frontier tensions, without resolving the underlying territorial disagreement.
- 6 February 2026: Washington and New Delhi announced a framework for an interim reciprocal trade agreement, demonstrating that economic friction has not eliminated their shared interests in strategic and technological cooperation.
- 27 January 2026: The European Union and India concluded free-trade negotiations; by September the Commission had submitted proposals for signature and conclusion, creating an additional channel for Indian economic diversification.
- 15 July 2026: The UK–India trade agreement entered into force, giving London a legally operative commercial framework distinct from the EU’s still-uncompleted approval process.
The decisive conclusion: A reduction in immediate Sino-Indian tensions should not be mistaken for the emergence of a China–India strategic alignment. The more defensible outlook is managed competition, contingent diplomatic cooperation and continuing efforts to reduce critical economic vulnerabilities.
The critical question for governments and industrial planners is whether stabilisation becomes institutionalised through verifiable border arrangements and more balanced commercial access, or remains vulnerable to renewed military incidents, trade restrictions and external geopolitical shocks.
Sources: Prime Minister’s Bilateral Meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping — Government of India — September 2026; President Xi Jinping Meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs — September 2026; United States–India Joint Statement — White House — February 2026.
China and India: The Industrial Dependence Behind Asia’s Diplomatic Rapprochement
Beijing and New Delhi are rebuilding political relations, but a $112 billion trade deficit, concentrated industrial supply chains and competing international partnerships reveal why economic power—not diplomatic alignment—will determine the next phase of Asian geopolitics.
The diplomatic recovery between China and India has exposed a contradiction neither government can resolve through political declarations. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping reaffirmed their commitment to bilateral stabilisation on 12 September 2026, yet India’s merchandise trade deficit with China had already reached $112.16 billion in the 2025–26 financial year. New Delhi is strengthening relationships with Washington, Moscow and European capitals while remaining deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks. Beijing, meanwhile, benefits from commercial relationships that India’s industrial expansion may actually reinforce. The central question is no longer whether the two Asian powers can restore dialogue. It is whether India can convert diplomatic autonomy into productive independence before the cost of industrial dependence begins to constrain its security, technology and foreign-policy decisions.
The $151 Billion Relationship That Gives Beijing Its Industrial Advantage
The figures published by the Indian Embassy in Beijing reveal the scale of the imbalance. Bilateral merchandise trade reached $151.10 billion in FY 2025–26, up from $127.71 billion the previous year. Indian imports from China increased to $131.63 billion, while Indian exports reached $19.47 billion. The resulting deficit widened from $99.21 billion to $112.16 billion despite a 36.62% increase in Indian exports.
Over the preceding decade, bilateral trade had more than doubled. Between FY 2016–17 and FY 2025–26, Indian imports from China increased from $61.28 billion to $131.63 billion, while the deficit rose from $51.11 billion to $112.16 billion. Approximately 87.1% of the latest bilateral trade value represented Chinese exports to India. The asymmetry is sufficiently large that even vigorous growth in Indian exports has failed to reverse the widening absolute deficit.
These figures do not prove that Beijing can dictate Indian policy. They reveal a more specific industrial imbalance. Chinese machinery, components, chemicals and intermediate goods contribute to production within India, including manufacturing intended for export to third markets. Restricting those supplies could therefore damage the same Indian industries that New Delhi is attempting to develop as alternatives to Chinese production.
The distinction changes the meaning of economic independence. A factory assembled in India may still require Chinese-origin production equipment, electronic components and specialised materials. Moving the final manufacturing stage does not necessarily transfer the upstream capabilities that determine costs, technological performance and continuity of supply.
India’s challenge is consequently not to eliminate Chinese imports indiscriminately. It is to identify the production stages whose interruption would impose disproportionate damage and build commercially viable alternatives. Without that distinction, import substitution risks becoming a tax on Indian industrial competitiveness rather than an instrument of national resilience.
The official figures, published by the Embassy of India in Beijing, place this dependency at the centre of the bilateral economic relationship.
Pharmaceuticals and Rare Earths Expose the Cost of Industrial Dependence
India’s pharmaceutical industry provides one of the clearest measurements of concentrated industrial exposure. According to the Department of Pharmaceuticals, the country imported $4.35 billion in active pharmaceutical ingredients, bulk drugs and intermediates in FY 2024–25, with China accounting for 73.71% of the relevant import value, or approximately $3.205 billion. The European Union supplied another 13.64%.
These figures concern defined pharmaceutical input categories rather than India’s entire medicines industry. Nevertheless, they identify a concrete vulnerability in production chains supporting antibiotics, cardiovascular treatments, oncology-related medicines and other therapeutic categories. A disruption involving a critical ingredient may interrupt downstream manufacturing even when its financial value represents a small proportion of the finished medicine.
New Delhi has begun investing against this exposure. Under the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Bulk Drugs, with an authorised outlay of ₹6,940 crore, 48 greenfield projects had been approved and 38 commissioned by December 2025. Actual reported investment reached ₹4,814.1 crore, with approximately 56,800 tonnes of annual manufacturing capacity created across commissioned projects.
The distinction between created capacity and usable output remains decisive. A commissioned chemical plant does not automatically eliminate import dependence: its products must meet technical specifications, regulatory requirements and commercial price conditions. The government’s own pharmaceutical industry implementation figures document progress, not completed national self-sufficiency.
Rare-earth materials expose the same difficulty at an earlier industrial stage. India’s government reported approximately 7.23 million tonnes of in-situ rare-earth oxide equivalent in monazite deposits, yet geological resources do not automatically provide the technology needed to produce refined metals, alloys and high-performance magnets.
The Sintered Rare-Earth Permanent Magnet Manufacturing Scheme, approved in November 2025, provides ₹7,280 crore and targets annual integrated capacity of 6,000 tonnes. By August 2026, the Ministry of Heavy Industries had received 20 bids for the programme. The tender process indicates commercial interest; it does not establish that the intended production capacity is operational.
The problem extends to batteries and electronics. In March 2026, the Ministry of Heavy Industries acknowledged that India’s lithium requirements for electric-vehicle batteries were entirely met through imports. Meanwhile, the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme, allocated ₹62,500 crore for FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31, and Semicon 2.0, allocated ₹1,27,500 crore, seek to deepen Indian manufacturing and technological capabilities.

Islamabad, Pakistan – Sitting with his elbows on his knees, Russia’s Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev leaned towards Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for talks in Rawalpindi on October 14.
While Kolokoltsev was in Pakistan, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), flew into Kabul to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq.
Officially, Russia, Pakistan and Afghanistan have issued little beyond standard statements about the meetings. But the signs are clear: Pakistan and Afghanistan have spent the past year exchanging fire and public threats. Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire in Doha last October and China hosted talks in Urumqi in April, but attacks inside Pakistan continued. Islamabad again struck Afghan territory in June, September and this month.
Russia now appears to be stepping in as a mediator.
Moscow’s special representative for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, told Russia’s TASS news agency earlier this month that his country was ready to play peace broker between Kabul and Islamabad if both sides requested it.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Russia, Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, said in March that Islamabad had approached Moscow. The Taliban, though, have not publicly requested Russian mediation, raising questions about how much and in what capacity Moscow can push Pakistan and Afghanistan to talks when other mediators have struggled.
A complicated history adds to the challenge Russia faces.
A diplomatic opening
Pakistan’s military media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said the Rawalpindi meeting discussed issues of “mutual interest and the regional security environment, with particular emphasis on strengthening bilateral security cooperation.”
The statement did not mention Afghanistan and neither Russian officials nor the Taliban have disclosed what the intelligence chiefs discussed. Moscow has, however, voiced concern about the fighting.
“We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children,” the Russian embassy in Kabul posted on X earlier this month.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said Pakistani strikes between September 30 and October 1 killed at least 10 civilians, mostly children.
In decades past, the idea of Russia mediating between Pakistan and the Taliban might have been unthinkable. Throughout the Cold War and even after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia was – and remains in many ways – one of the closest strategic and military partners of India, the neighbour Pakistan has fought multiple wars against. While in Afghanistan, Russia backed the Northern Alliance against the Taliban throughout the 1990s.
But in recent years, Russia has significantly strengthened relations with both Pakistan and the Taliban. Then Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was in Moscow when Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022. Last year, Russia became the first country in the world to officially recognise the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
Those shifts have been driven by Russia’s desire to broaden its options in South Asia, at a time when India has embraced the United States and to counter the rise of the Afghan branch of ISIL, also known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or ISKP. While the Taliban are concerned with ruling Afghanistan, ISKP has broader territorial ambitions and carried out an attack in Moscow in 2024 that killed nearly 150 people. The Taliban and the ISKP are sworn enemies.
Fighting between Pakistan and the Taliban created regional instability and Moscow was worried that could make it easier for armed groups to spill into Central Asia, said Taimur Khan, a research associate at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI).
“Mediation also helps Moscow preserve its regional influence and avoid a vacuum that could invite renewed extra-regional involvement,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why mediation stalled
Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban in Doha last October, but talks in Istanbul collapsed the following month and skirmishes resumed. Islamabad also launched air raids inside Afghanistan. China hosted talks in Urumqi in April.
In mid-September, Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, met Taliban officials in Kabul and Kandahar before travelling to Islamabad.
An attack in Kohat followed on September 18, with Pakistan striking Afghanistan on September 24 and October 1.
“Other actors have so far achieved more tangible mediation results in this conflict,” Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Central Asia analyst and head of research at the geopolitical foresight agency, Nightingale Int, told Al Jazeera.
Russia’s own effort stalled at a Moscow meeting on October 5.
Kabulov told TASS that the Afghan delegation objected to Afghanistan being mentioned too often in connection with “terrorism”.
“For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said on October 9 at a weekly media briefing.
Kabul-based security analyst Tameem Bahiss said the objection reflected Kabul’s longstanding position.
“Accepting language that repeatedly associates Afghanistan with terrorism could be seen as an acknowledgement of the very allegations Kabul has consistently denied,” he told Al Jazeera.
The TTP problem
At the Moscow meeting, Pakistan’s special representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, said “terrorism” remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said the two countries’ problems could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, according to Afghan media.
Pakistan says the Pakistani Taliban and other armed groups shelter in Afghanistan.
Kabul rejects the allegation, saying it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries and that Pakistan’s security problems are largely internal, Bahiss said.
Moscow’s public warnings have focused on the ISKP.
“There is no visible public pressure from Russia on the Taliban over Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and Moscow is unlikely to exert such pressure,” Gusseinov said. TTP is the official name of the Pakistani Taliban, which is behind dozens of the deadliest attacks Pakistan has suffered in recent years.
He argued that pressing the Taliban hard on Pakistan’s behalf would undermine Moscow’s standing as a neutral mediator and its partnership with the Taliban against ISKP.
“Russia’s primary concern is ISKP and it appears satisfied with the Taliban’s efforts to counter the group,” Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based analyst specialising in armed groups and security dynamics in Afghanistan and Pakistan, told Al Jazeera.
What Moscow brings
Still, Russia has something earlier mediators did not. In July 2025, it became the only country to recognise the Taliban government.
Taimur Khan said that could give Moscow another source of influence.
“The Taliban authorities’ interest in preserving that recognition and expanding cooperation with Moscow could give Russia additional influence in seeking action against the TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan,” he said.
In May, the two sides signed an unpublished military-technical agreement covering, according to Kabulov, the repair and maintenance of equipment the Taliban already hold, mostly Soviet and Russian-made.
Three days after the signing, the Taliban’s Defence Minister, Mohammad Yaqoob, said Pakistan would soon no longer dare to launch strikes.
On June 9 and 10, Pakistani aircraft struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika provinces, killing 13 civilians, according to the Afghan government.
“Russia has greater access to the Taliban than any other major power, but its actual leverage is considerably more limited than is often assumed,” analyst Gusseinov said.
Sayed said senior Taliban leaders continued visiting Russia and India as fighting escalated, seemingly signalling they could offset Pakistan’s military superiority through new alignments.
“While the military and political significance of these ties remains unclear, the Taliban present such diplomatic developments to the Afghan public, particularly their supporters, as political achievements that reinforce their image of strength,” he said.
Why the SCO matters
Pakistan chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) for 2026-27 and will host the 10-member bloc’s summit in Islamabad next year.
The Taliban were not invited to this year’s summit in Bishkek, where members called for an inclusive government in Kabul.
On July 16, then-Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Afghanistan first needed diplomatic relations with member states, when asked whether Pakistan was blocking its inclusion in the SCO.
In September, Tirmizi, the Pakistani envoy in Moscow, said he did not see full SCO membership for Afghanistan as an option under the current Taliban government.
“The chairmanship strengthens Moscow’s reasons to invest in its relationship with Pakistan and manage differences over Afghanistan constructively,” Taimur Khan said.
The Foreign Office did not answer Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the Taliban would be invited next year.
“I cannot recall an instance where Kabul has explicitly requested Moscow to mediate between the two countries,” Bahiss said. “Nevertheless, Kabul’s repeated calls for diplomacy and its relatively close relations with Russia suggest that it would likely welcome Russian mediation if Moscow offered to play such a role.”

articles.full_text:
The NQM is one of nine initiatives under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Science, Technology Innovation Advisory Council (PMSTIAC), aimed at positioning India as a global leader in quantum technology.
"The first phase of NM-ICPS is ending in December 2027, and we are thinking of the second phase, which combines with physical artificial intelligence (AI)," Umesh V Waghmare, secretary, Department of Science & Technology (DST), told ETTelecom, adding that the fine print would depend on the specific technologies and products to be demonstrated in the coming year.
In December 2018, the Cabinet approved the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS) for an initial five-year term with an outlay of ₹3,660 crore. Union Minister Jitendra Singh-led Department of Science & Technology is implementing this Mission.
"The National Quantum Mission (NQM) is the youngest. We are in the third year now, and it has done a brilliant job in certain directions. In quantum communication, we have made good leaps. DST supports exploratory research," Waghmare said.
In April 2023, the Cabinet approved NQM for the 2023–24 to 2030–31 period with a budget allocation of ₹6,003.65 crore.
The NQM is one of nine initiatives under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Science, Technology Innovation Advisory Council (PMSTIAC), aimed at positioning India as a global leader in quantum technology.
Under the national program, dedicated efforts are underway to develop quantum-resilient encryption techniques and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) frameworks, ensuring the safety and sovereignty of the country's critical database systems in the quantum era.
"One of our mandates and emphasis is the translation of research into real-world products and applications, and that was historically a weak part in the Indian community, but the department was actually very visionary."
Over the last few years, the research and development (R&D) spend of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) witnessed a growth of 85% to ₹2.45 trillion in 2023–24, from ₹1.33 trillion in 2019–20.
India aims to take R&D investment to 2% of the GDP by 2035.
The Technology, Translation and Innovation (TTI) division under the department has been actively engaged across the entire value chain, and supports moderate funding. "If you want to now scale up and make real-world applications and products which will be sold globally, then you need industries to come in and invest."
To further engage with the industry, the Research and Development Innovation Fund (RDIF), a ₹1 lakh-crore corpus in the form of a long-term loan or equity, is conceived, he said, adding that the government is aggressively focusing on deep tech enablement.
Waghmare further said that quantum communication is one of the major outcomes, following the demonstration of a 1,000-kilometer network, and efforts are underway to also demonstrate a 2,000-kilometer quantum communication network.
The milestone was achieved using an indigenous Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) network developed by QNu Labs, a Bengaluru-based deep-tech startup.

articles.title: Pakistan Plans More Panda Bond Sales in China - The Daily CPEC
articles.summary: Pakistan Plans More Panda Bond Sales in China  The Daily CPEC
articles.full_text:
Pakistan plans to issue more Panda bonds in China as it seeks to become a regular sovereign borrower in the country’s domestic capital market, according to a government statement.
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb discussed the plans with Chinese Finance Minister Lan Fo’an on October 15 in Bangkok. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the World Bank Group-IMF Annual Meetings.
The two ministers reviewed Pakistan’s first Panda bond issuance and explored plans for further fundraising in China.
Pakistan Seeks Regular Access to China’s Bond Market
Aurangzeb highlighted progress towards macroeconomic stability, while Lan welcomed Pakistan’s renewed access to international capital markets.
Pakistan’s inaugural Panda bond carried a coupon rate of 2.5 per cent and received credit enhancement from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). The government said the offering attracted strong investor demand.
Aurangzeb said Pakistan wanted the first issuance to establish a foundation for regular bond sales. He also expressed interest in continued AIIB support for future offerings.
Panda bonds allow foreign governments and companies to raise funds in China’s domestic bond market, with proceeds generally denominated in Chinese yuan.
Further Pakistani issuances will depend on market conditions, borrowing costs and the country’s debt sustainability.
Ministers Discuss Eurobond Market Return
The meeting also covered Pakistan’s planned return to the Eurobond market after a four-year gap.
Access to both Chinese and international capital markets could broaden Pakistan’s financing options. However, the terms and timing of future borrowing will remain important for managing debt costs and financial risks.
SCO Finance Cooperation and Development Bank
The ministers discussed Pakistan’s chairmanship of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) and preparations for an upcoming summit in Islamabad.
They also reviewed plans for an SCO finance ministers’ meeting in the Pakistani capital. Lan said he intended to attend the meeting.
Both sides discussed a proposed SCO Development Bank. China encouraged Pakistan to participate in consultations and help build consensus on the initiative.
Aurangzeb reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for establishing the proposed institution.
China-Pakistan Connectivity and Digital Cooperation
Lan also referred to progress towards consensus on proposed route changes for a China-Pakistan highway project.
Aurangzeb briefed his Chinese counterpart on Pakistan’s engagement with Alibaba on digital transformation and artificial intelligence skills training. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to implementing the existing cooperation framework.
The discussions reflect the wider scope of Pakistan-China economic engagement, covering financial markets, regional cooperation, transport connectivity and digital skills development.

articles.title: Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's reliance on US tech, Europe admits 'can't replace capability' - The Times of India
articles.summary: Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's reliance on US tech, Europe admits 'can't replace capability'  The Times of India'Neither Me Nor Musk': Trump Denies Role In Ukraine Losing Starlink Access  NDTVEXCLUSIVE: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say  ReutersDon’t Get Starstruck By Musk  The Times of IndiaStarlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
European Union leaders are grappling with how to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system after disruptions to its services raised concerns about Kyiv’s reliance on US-controlled technology for battlefield operations.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe did not have an immediate alternative to the satellite network, which has become essential to Ukraine’s military communications, as leaders gathered for a summit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also in attendance.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can't replace this capability," Kallas said before the talks.
She added that the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked and needed to develop, stressing that the gaps had to be addressed "as soon as possible".
The issue has gained urgency after Ukrainian officials reported restrictions and slower speeds on parts of the Starlink system this week, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Trump’s deal involving Russian diesel.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to refrain from attacking Russian refineries and announced a truce on energy infrastructure attacks. However, Ukraine has continued to target Russian refineries.
Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government rather than his company, SpaceX.
Ukraine uses Starshield, the military-grade satellite service, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses Starlink’s civilian satellite network, but not for offensive operations.
European leaders call for stronger satellite capabilities
Several European leaders acknowledged that building an alternative to Starlink would take time, even as the latest disruptions highlighted the need to strengthen the continent’s satellite communications capacity.
"Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters.
"It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have, but not enough. So this is strategically something we have to discuss today."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide similar services in the near future.
British defence minister Wes Streeting also said he had raised Starlink with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, on Thursday.
"It's not yet clear to us in the UK what happened, why the service interruption occurred. But I am reassured, and was reassured directly by Secretary Hegseth, that the service has been restored," Streeting told the BBC on Friday.
Ukrainian officials reported slower speeds on the system on Wednesday, affecting connectivity.
Some Ukrainian officials suggested Washington was behind the restrictions reported on certain Starlink internet terminals.
Eutelsat shares jump as investors look to European alternatives
The disruption has renewed investor interest in European satellite operators that could help reduce reliance on SpaceX.
Shares in Eutelsat, the French satellite operator that runs the OneWeb network, rose 12 per cent on Friday, taking its gains for the week to 23 per cent. Paris-listed SES, another European satellite operator, gained 6.7 per cent.
The gains followed a Reuters report citing two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter, which said an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House.
Analysts said the developments had strengthened the case for European satellite operators as governments increasingly sought alternatives to US technology.
"The Starlink Ukrainian issue helped," Oddo BHF analyst Stéphane Beyazian said of the share price movements, according to Reuters.
"But more generally, shares have been done so much due to the Starlink risk — now investors are reconsidering them as the European industry will not disappear to Starlink," he added.
Eutelsat operates OneWeb, a network of around 600 low-Earth orbit satellites that provides broadband connectivity to governments, airlines and telecommunications operators. Backed by the French and British governments, OneWeb is widely viewed as Europe's leading challenger to Starlink, whose much larger satellite network dominates the global low-Earth orbit broadband market.
Eutelsat chief executive Jean-François Fallacher said in March that the company had sold its entire capacity in Ukraine. The company operates as a dual-use provider, with thousands of antennas active and devices capable of operating in environments affected by GPS jamming, Reuters reported.
However, analysts cautioned that European systems could not immediately match Starlink's capabilities.
"We don’t see (Europe's IRIS² satellite project) fully replicating Starlink’s capabilities in the short term, although SES and Eutelsat can already provide complementary satellite connectivity," ING analyst Jan Frederik Slijkerman said.
Ukraine’s reliance on Starlink exposes a strategic vulnerability
Starlink has played a central role in Ukraine’s war effort since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukraine’s then deputy prime minister and digital transformation minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, publicly appealed to Musk for connectivity in the early days of the invasion. The first 500 Starlink terminals arrived in Ukraine two days later, and Musk subsequently granted the Ukrainian government and military access to the network, initially free of charge.
The system has enabled secure communications between Ukrainian military units and supported command, control, intelligence and surveillance operations. Its connectivity has also been particularly important to Ukraine’s extensive use of drones.
However, the relationship has faced tensions over the years. In 2022, Musk refused a Ukrainian request to activate Starlink connectivity for a planned operation near Crimea, saying that doing so would make SpaceX explicitly complicit in a major act of war and risk escalating the conflict.
More recently, Musk said Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the US government, with decisions on restrictions ultimately resting with the US military and the US president.
The latest disruption has again drawn attention to the risks of Ukraine relying on a satellite network controlled by a private company whose military services are subject to US government decisions.
For European leaders, the immediate challenge remains how to maintain Ukraine’s communications capabilities while developing alternative systems.

articles.title: Highway Projects Awarded Rise 62.9%, Air Cargo Traffic Grows 12%: MoSPI - DD India
articles.summary: Highway Projects Awarded Rise 62.9%, Air Cargo Traffic Grows 12%: MoSPI  DD India
articles.full_text:
India’s infrastructure sector has recorded growth across highways, aviation, telecommunications, ports and power, according to the latest quarterly update of the PAIMANA Performance Monitoring Dashboard released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).
The dashboard highlights a 62.9 per cent year-on-year increase in National Highway projects awarded during April–September of the current financial year, while air cargo traffic rose 12 per cent to 18.6 lakh tonnes during April–August.
Launched on April 16, 2026, the PAIMANA dashboard provides a unified digital platform for monitoring infrastructure performance and supporting evidence-based policymaking. The latest update expands the dashboard to 184 indicators, including 21 newly added indicators. Quarterly data has also been updated for 41 indicators across power, civil aviation, ports, shipping and waterways, and road transport and highways.
The dashboard tracks six infrastructure sub-sectors: civil aviation, road transport and highways, power, ports, shipping and waterways, telecommunications, and railways. Its indicators are organised around five dimensions: access, quality, fiscal cost and revenue, utilisation, and affordability.
Highways and Digital Connectivity Expand
The road transport and highways sector recorded 2,236.3 kilometres of National Highway projects awarded during April–September 2026–27, registering year-on-year growth of 62.9 per cent.
Electronic toll collection also recorded an increase, with transactions reaching 225.2 crore during the period, up 24.1 per cent year-on-year. The value of electronic toll collection stood at ₹36,994.5 crore, registering growth of 11.7 per cent.
In telecommunications, India’s cumulative optical fibre cable network reached 7,52,113 kilometres by August 2026, following the addition of 29,256 kilometres during April–August.
Wired broadband subscribers grew 12.4 per cent and wireless broadband subscribers increased 12.9 per cent in 2025–26. The number of connected Gram Panchayats reached 2,23,814 by August 2026, with 5,352 added during the first five months of the current financial year.
Air Cargo and Port Traffic Register Growth
The civil aviation sector handled 18.6 lakh tonnes of air cargo during April–August 2026–27, marking a year-on-year increase of 12 per cent. Delhi airport handled the highest volume, at 5.3 lakh tonnes.
Foreign tourist arrivals reached 30.49 lakh up to August in the current financial year, registering 2 per cent growth compared with the corresponding period a year earlier.
At major ports, cargo handling increased 7.2 per cent to 390.4 million tonnes during April–August 2026–27. Non-major ports recorded growth of 1.8 per cent, handling 313.4 million tonnes during the same period.
Petroleum and crude products accounted for approximately 29.2 per cent of cargo handled at major ports, remaining the largest commodity category. Cargo movement in this category increased 3.1 per cent year-on-year.
Power Capacity and Renewable Energy Growth
India’s total installed power capacity reached 5,32,739.7 megawatts in 2025–26, registering year-on-year growth of 12.1 per cent.
Renewable energy capacity increased 29.5 per cent to 2,23,273 megawatts, accounting for approximately 42 per cent of the country’s total installed power capacity.
The figures highlight the growing contribution of renewable energy sources to India’s overall electricity generation capacity.
Railways Strengthen Infrastructure Capacity
Indian Railways also recorded growth in infrastructure and rolling stock. During 2024–25, the number of coaches increased 4.5 per cent and locomotives rose 6.4 per cent.
The length of electrified railway tracks increased 4.8 per cent, while the number of railway wagons grew 5.4 per cent during the same financial year.
MoSPI said the PAIMANA Performance Monitoring Dashboard would continue to be updated quarterly to improve transparency, facilitate access to official infrastructure statistics and support informed decision-making.
The next quarterly update is scheduled for January 15, 2027. The dashboard is available at paimana-perf.mospi.gov.in.

articles.title: Innovation is key to a more resilient food future for Bangladesh - The Daily Star
articles.summary: Innovation is key to a more resilient food future for Bangladesh  The Daily Star
articles.full_text:
Behind every plate of rice, dal, vegetables, and fish in Bangladesh is the work of farmers, fishers, livestock keepers, and food workers. Their decisions, and ours as consumers, influence how we manage land and water, safeguard biodiversity, respond to climate change, and create livelihood opportunities for the next generation. This year’s World Food Day theme, “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”, calls on us to bring science, technology, and traditional knowledge together to secure a healthier, more sustainable food future. Innovation takes many forms: a farmer adopting a climate resilient crop variety, a producer receiving timely weather advice, or a woman accessing finance to grow her enterprise.
Over decades, farmers’ ingenuity, supported by research, irrigation, improved varieties, mechanisation, and extension services, has transformed production despite growing pressure on natural resources and exposure to climate and economic shocks. Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) September 2026 Global Information and Early Warning System brief forecasts aggregate paddy production for 2026-27 at 61.9 million tonnes, about 5 percent over the last five-year average. But higher production alone cannot guarantee better nutrition or greater prosperity. Progress must also be measured by whether families can afford diverse, safe, and nutritious diets, whether producers earn decent incomes, and whether food systems withstand shocks. Only 39 percent of women meet minimum dietary diversity, a sign that many diets still lack variety.
Bangladesh must therefore connect agricultural productivity more firmly with nutrition, livelihoods, and environmental sustainability. That means protecting soil health, water, and biodiversity while increasing returns for farmers and rural entrepreneurs. It requires bringing science and data to the field faster, expanding access to climate-resilient and salt tolerant varieties, strengthening timely advisory services, and building producer organisations that help smallholders negotiate better prices. The ambition is to turn innovation into better diets, stronger livelihoods, and a more resilient future.
Working with the government, FAO, World Food Programme (WFP), and International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) support access to agricultural information, finance, essential services, and market, helping farmers turn innovation into practical gains. In coastal, drought-prone, and char areas, farmers are growing nutritious vegetables year-round through solar-powered irrigation, improved seedling production, and off-season cultivation. Adoption of climate-resilient technologies has reached 86 percent among participating farmers, exceeding by 35 percent adoption among comparable farmers outside the initiatives.
Sensor-based fishpond monitoring, smart irrigation, solar drying, and blockchain-based traceability offer further opportunities to conserve resources, improve production, reduce losses, and access higher-value markets. Combined with finance, training, and nutrition education, these innovations can strengthen livelihoods, improve diets, and expand opportunities for women farmers.
Protecting these gains is equally urgent as floods, cyclones, salinity, drought, and river erosion can quickly undermine years of progress. About 18.1 million people in Bangladesh are projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity between September and December 2026. Preparedness must therefore be central to agrifood investment. Early warning and anticipatory action can deliver cash and advice before a flood strike, helping families protect their assets and livelihoods. Digital assistance platforms, early warning systems, vulnerability analysis, and nutrition-sensitive programmes can further strengthen the speed and targeting of support.
Strong public systems are essential to bring these benefits to scale. The government’s Farmer Card and electronic voucher system provide a foundation for delivering support more transparently. By enabling eligible farmers to redeem subsidies for approved agricultural inputs, these tools can improve subsidy targeting and reduce leakage.
Three priorities should guide the next phase. First, connecting weather alerts, agricultural advice, market information, and input support through accessible digital services linked to the Farmer Card platform. Second, combining public, private, and development finance to scale innovations with demonstrated results. We know that there have been income gains of 64 percent where the private sector is engaged, four times those recorded where it is not, highlighting the importance of effective market partnerships. Third, making nutrition an explicit investment objective by supporting production that both nourishes families and generates reliable income.
Success will depend on whether these opportunities reach small producers, including women, young people, and those in remote or climate-vulnerable communities. A smartphone may help a farmer receive a weather alert, find a buyer, or secure working capital. Its real value, however, is the confidence and opportunity it gives a farmer to make better decisions and build a more secure future. For Bangladesh, nourishing tomorrow means producing better, wasting less and making healthy diets more affordable. The government, financial institutions, researchers, businesses, and development partners must work together to bring proven solutions within reach of every small producer.
On World Food Day, the task is to turn the innovation already taking root across Bangladesh into lasting progress. By connecting science with local knowledge, investment with inclusion, and productivity with nutrition, we can build stronger livelihoods, more resilient communities, and a healthier future for Bangladesh.
Jiaoqun Shi is a FAO representative.
Valantine Achancho is country director and representative at IFAD.
Coco Ushiyama is resident representative and country director at WFP.

Protesters carrying the national flag faced detention across Central Delhi, including student leaders Neha Bora and Dipankar Bhattacharya marching from Mandi House. Authorities shut Central Park for two days and deployed extensive security to prevent unauthorised gatherings, while maintaining regular metro services and traffic flow. Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken into preventive custody from the residence of NCP SP spokesperson Anish Gawande after Delhi Police denied permission for his demonstration. Police served notices prohibiting the rally, citing concerns over public order, though Dipke argued that unfurling the national flag was peaceful and constitutional. Continued attempts by demonstrators to converge at the inner circle of Connaught Place led to sustained police action and reignited debate concerning democratic assembly rights.
Political Row Over Destabilisation Charges, Urban Naxal Claims And Anarchy Allegations
A political confrontation has erupted following statements concerning regime change and organised protests. Charges have been raised asserting that the opposition is pursuing an urban Naxal agenda to destabilise the country in collusion with foreign forces. Accusations have also been made regarding attempts to seize power at any cost and sowing anarchy to weaken national stability amid ongoing political debates.
LATEST VIDEOS
Delhi witnessed intense activity as police initiated detentions following protests and a Tiranga rally called by the CJP and left-backed groups across Connaught Place, Mandi House, and Jantar Mantar.
A major political row has erupted over Dr Seema Khanna, the Election Commission of India's Director General of Information Technology, following remarks by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi questioning her presence in Dehradun. Khanna, who joined the poll body on deputation from the National Informatics Centre in 2025, oversees digital infrastructure including ECINet and ERONet. Concerns were raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi over whether Electoral Registration Officers had adequate software access to manage and correct voter lists independently. The Election Commission clarified Khanna was in Dehradun overseeing election preparedness for Uttarakhand's upcoming assembly polls, amid opposition scrutiny over voter data transparency.
The Delhi Police has denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site amid ongoing demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise. Protests have now been redirected to three alternative locations: Ramlila Maidan, the CBD Ground in Shahdara, and Burari Ground. However, two of these newly designated venues are situated significantly farther away from Parliament and central administrative offices, with CBD Ground approximately fourteen kilometres away and Burari Ground nearly twenty-three kilometres away. Moving demonstrations away from the corridors of power introduces logistical challenges, including massive crowd capacities ranging from fifteen thousand to eighty thousand people, expensive booking fees, and mandatory police clearance. Critics point out that shifting demonstrations far from the political centre may isolate demonstrators from policymakers, the media, and spontaneous public participation.

New facility at the MAHE Bengaluru campus to strengthen quantum engineering, research, innovation and workforce development
Bengaluru, October 16, 2026: Manipal Institute of Technology, Bengaluru (MIT Bengaluru), today launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE. Established by Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), an Institution of Eminence Deemed to be University, this initiative will advance quantum hardware experimentation, engineering education and indigenous technology development in alignment with India’s National Quantum Mission.
The facility was inaugurated by chief guest Dr. Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist & Co-Founder, Zoho Corp, Guest of Honour Dr. Marcus Rommel, CTO, ConScience in the presence of Dr. Sharath K. Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE, Lieutenant General (Dr.) M. D. Venkatesh, VSM (Retd.) 7th Vice Chancellor MAHE and Advisor to MEMG, Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru, Dr. Karunakar A Kotegar, Pro Vice Chancellor, Technology & Science, MAHE, Dr. Raghavendra Prabhu, Additional Registrar, MAHE Bengaluru, Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru and Mr. Vishal Chatrath, Co-Founder & CEO, QuantrolOX.
Located at the MAHE Bengaluru campus, Quantum facility at MIT BLRU provides students, researchers and industry collaborators with hands on access to advanced quantum computing infrastructure, including quantum hardware, cryogenic systems and quantum control technologies. Through an integrated academic framework, the facility will support experimentation, application development, deep-tech start-up incubation, component innovation, testing and translational research, positioning MIT Bengaluru as an emerging centre for quantum engineering and indigenous hardware development.
The facility commences operations with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system designed for advanced training and experimentation. This marks the first phase of a structured roadmap progressing from sub-50-qubit training systems to 150-qubit proof-of-concept platforms and, ultimately, to industrial-grade quantum product systems with more than 1,000 qubits.
Ahead of the launch, faculty members and students from the Bengaluru and Manipal campuses completed specialised training at the MIT Bengaluru campus and the QuantrolOx laboratory at QuTech, TU Delft, in the Netherlands. The programme developed practical capabilities in dilution refrigerator assembly, cryogenic systems, quantum control technologies, QPU measurements and superconducting quantum hardware, preparing the team to support the operations of Quantum facility at MIT BLRU.
The facility will support learning and research in areas such as healthcare, pharmaceuticals, oncology, aerospace and advanced computing. It will also strengthen MIT Bengaluru’s collaboration with industry and research organisations while developing a future ready talent pipeline in quantum technologies.
The initiative has been formalised through Memorandums of Agreement with QuantrolOx of Finland, in association with Bluefors of Finland, Qblox of the Netherlands and ConScience of Sweden. These collaborations establish a first year roadmap focused on workforce development, hardware experimentation, intellectual property co development and national testing infrastructure.
As part of its workforce development efforts, the Quantum facility at MIT, Bengaluru aims to train 100 quantum engineers by December 2026. It will also conduct quantum awareness programmes, summer and winter camps for Class 10 and Class 12 students across rural India, short hands-on exposure programmes and capacity-building initiatives for technical professionals.
The facility will provide researchers, start-ups and industry partners with access to advanced quantum testing and measurement infrastructure, strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, innovation and India’s growing quantum technology ecosystem.

Dr. Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist & Co-Founder, Zoho Corp, said, “Q-HUB is a place for students to dream, think deeply and turn their ideas into conviction and action. Just as personal computers & internet transformed possibilities for my generation, quantum computing can empower this generation to build new machines, create breakthrough applications and take India to greater heights.”
Dr. Sharath K Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE, said, “The MAHE House of Quantum at MIT, Bengaluru reflects MAHE’s commitment to building advanced scientific capabilities and nurturing talent in emerging technologies. By creating access to modern quantum infrastructure, we aim to contribute meaningfully to India’s growing quantum ecosystem.”
Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru, said, “The Hub brings together education, research and innovation on a common platform. It will create opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and help translate academic research into real world technological impact.”
Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru, said, “The Quantum facility at MIT, Bengaluru will provide students and researchers with valuable exposure to real quantum systems and engineering environments. It marks an important step towards developing the next generation of quantum scientists, engineers and innovators.“

articles.title: Japan issued alert for 'largest recorded' 9.9 magnitude earthquake, but ground didn't shake: What happene - The Times of India
articles.summary: Japan issued alert for 'largest recorded' 9.9 magnitude earthquake, but ground didn't shake: What happene  The Times of IndiaEarthquake of magnitude 7 strikes Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, EMSC says  ReutersEarthquake of 6.9 magnitude hits near Ozernovskiy in Russia  The HinduJapan Meteorological Agency Cancels Earthquake Early Warning in Many Areas (UPDATE 1)  The Japan NewsEarthquake Of Magnitude 7 Strikes Russia, Japan Mistakenly Issues 9.9 Warning&nbsp...
articles.full_text:
Japan triggered widespread alarm on Friday after its earthquake early warning system "announced" a magnitude-9.9 earthquake alert, prompting emergency phone alerts, public loudspeaker warnings and television broadcasts urging people to take shelter, before the warning was withdrawn eight minutes later.
However, no major shaking followed the alert, which the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) later attributed to errors in its earthquake magnitude estimation and location calculations. The agency is investigating the cause of the malfunction, reportd Japan Times.
The alert was issued at 12.40 pm (local time), two minutes after a magnitude-6.9 earthquake struck off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The warning incorrectly placed the epicentre near the Kuril Islands and predicted seismic intensity of up to shindo 7, the highest level on Japan's seven-point seismic intensity scale, across areas stretching from Hokkaido to the Tokai region.
In Japan, however, the recorded shaking reached only shindo 1, a level at which vibrations may be barely noticeable. At 12.48 pm (local time), the JMA issued a cancellation notice, marking the first time an emergency earthquake warning had been formally withdrawn, according to the agency.
The predicted magnitude of 9.9 also drew attention because it exceeded the magnitude of any earthquake recorded in history. The 1960 earthquake off Chile's Biobio region, the strongest on record, measured magnitude 9.5. 
The JMA said 9.9 was the highest magnitude its system could communicate externally.
Ayataka Ebita, head of the JMA's earthquake and tsunami observation division, said the system had mistakenly estimated the earthquake's epicentre and overstated its magnitude. The agency ruled out a cyberattack and said it was examining how the error occurred.
At a subsequent briefing, the JMA said the system had applied a magnitude formula designed for earthquakes within Japan to a quake occurring far away. It had also used different estimated locations to calculate the magnitude and forecast shaking, although both calculations should have been based on the same location.
The investigation is continuing. Ebita said lightning was not believed to have caused the error, adding that the processing of seismic sensor data could have contributed to the malfunction.
In Tokyo on Friday, pedestrians paused to check their phones as warnings circulated, while users of the NERV Disaster Prevention app received a magnitude-9.9 alert accompanied by a countdown to shaking that never materialised.
Lola Milroy-Tompkins, a 20-year-old British student at Waseda University in Tokyo, said she was eating lunch in a campus cafeteria when the alarm sounded.
“I have never experienced an earthquake before and I expected the grand style shaking and everything to start falling around me,” she said.
She recalled students worrying and talking among themselves as they tried to understand what was happening, but the anticipated earthquake never arrived.
The JMA's early warning system automatically combines readings from seismometers at observation stations to estimate an earthquake's location, magnitude and expected intensity. Ebita said the reliability of such estimates depends on the number of observation stations and the quality of their readings, which can deteriorate when an earthquake occurs far from monitoring equipment.
The incident also disrupted public transport. The Tokaido Shinkansen line was halted for 15 minutes after an automated safety system was triggered, Central Japan Railway said. Government officials reported no damage related to the Kamchatka earthquake.
Chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara said the government took seriously the anxiety caused by the warning and the burden on people who evacuated or took precautionary measures, as well as those whose travel and business activities were disrupted.
False alarms have occurred previously. In July 2020, the JMA issued a warning covering 15 prefectures, including Tokyo, after incorrectly estimating an earthquake's location and magnitude. In August 2013, noise from a seabed seismometer was mistakenly combined with readings from a small earthquake, triggering widespread warnings across the Kinki region. Neither incident produced shaking of shindo 1 or higher, according to the JMA.
The agency's website noted that false alarms can result from sensor noise caused by accidents, lightning or equipment failures.

articles.title: Dr Doom, who predicted global financial crisis, has a forecast for India - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Dr Doom, who predicted global financial crisis, has a forecast for India  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
By treating the US financial system not as an immune superpower but as a troubled emerging market burdened by a massive current account deficit, Roubini warned that loose lending standards, rampant subprime mortgages, and high household debt would trigger widespread defaults. He correctly predicted that the ensuing housing bubble burst would freeze mortgage-backed securities, collapse major banks and mortgage lenders, and ultimately spark a severe global recession through highly interconnected international financial markets.
Also Read: Markets will push the US to act constructively: Nouriel Roubini
The crisis that erupted in 2008 gave his warning a remarkable degree of vindication.
Roubini now sees another major economic shift taking shape, but a positive one. In an interview with ET, he said India was a “major success story with the potential to become an even bigger one” and that the next few decades could be about India as much as the past several decades were about China.
Why America may eventually soften its tariff stance
Roubini said in the ET interview: “Markets will force the US to adopt a more constructive approach, including towards India.” He said Washington needed to recognise that maintaining good relations with India, including on trade, was critical and fundamental. He expects US tariffs to fall further as inflation and affordability concerns put pressure on American policymakers. “India is a huge and rising economy and is aligned with many of the objectives of the US and the West…Rationality will prevail,” he said. He expects US tariffs to fall further from 9% amid concerns around inflation and affordability.
The commercial stakes are already visible in the numbers. India's exports to the US rose to $42.79 billion between April and August, compared with $40.39 billion in the same period a year earlier. A trade deal could strengthen this momentum by improving access for Indian manufacturers and giving American businesses a clearer framework for expanding in India.
Roubini's point is that the relationship has an economic logic that tariff disputes cannot erase indefinitely. Lower trade barriers would benefit both economies, while India's growing weight in global commerce gives Washington an additional reason to pursue a stable partnership.
Also Read: India is now biggest country exposure for Fairfax, we have zero bets on AI: Prem Watsa
India is a bright spot in a changing global economy
“India is a major success story with the potential to become an even bigger one,” Roubini told ET. He cited the country's large domestic market, talent pool, macroeconomic fundamentals and commitment to opening up to the world. With further reforms, he believes potential growth could exceed 8%.
Roubini's observations are based on the fact that India's appeal lies partly in its combination of domestic demand and opportunities to expand its role in international trade. A growing consumer market creates room for businesses across manufacturing, financial services, technology and infrastructure. At the same time, India's established services-export industry provides a platform for moving into higher-value activities. In parallel, India is ramping up its manufacturing with huge incentives and trying to get a foothold in the global value chain, even as global giants are setting up or expanding capacity in India.
India's trade diplomacy is moving in the same direction. Agreements with the UK and other partners can widen market access for Indian businesses and make the country a more attractive base for export-oriented investment.
For Roubini, the combination of domestic demand, an expanding industrial base and greater integration with global markets puts India in a favourable position. Continued reforms could help turn that position into a sustained period of faster growth.
India needs to accelerate growth to create jobs
“Growth of 7% is not enough. India needs to get closer to 9% to ensure that young people can secure good jobs,” Roubini told ET. He warned that AI would reshape employment across both manual and cognitive occupations, making it harder to rely on population growth alone as an economic advantage.
Roubini's observation aligns with a general realisation that the employment challenge is central to India's next phase of development. Millions of young people will enter the workforce over the coming years. Faster economic growth can expand the number of available jobs, but the country will need sectors capable of employing workers at scale.
Manufacturing is particularly important because it can generate jobs beyond the highly skilled roles concentrated in technology and professional services. Electronics, automobiles, textiles and other export-oriented industries can create employment across production, logistics and supplier networks. Their expansion can also raise productivity and help workers move into better-paid occupations. The AI transition adds urgency to this task.
Higher growth would give businesses more room to invest and expand hiring. Better vocational training and stronger links between education and industry could help workers access the resulting opportunities. Roubini's call for growth closer to 9% reflects the scale of the employment ambition India must pursue as technology transforms the workplace.
Friendshoring could give India a larger role
“Geopolitics benefits India because China is increasingly considered risky,” Roubini told ET. He expects nearshoring and friendshoring to encourage manufacturers to diversify away from China. He said India was less exposed to external shocks and global uncertainty given its large domestic market, while China’s growth was trending downwards because of demographic challenges, excessive leverage, and issues in the real estate sector.
Roubini is right because companies are increasingly looking to spread production across more locations rather than concentrate it in a single country. This creates an opening for India, especially in electronics, automobiles and semiconductor-related industries, where global businesses are looking to build additional capacity.
India's electronics industry, for instance, is moving up the supply chain. Indian electronics exports to China rose almost 40% in the five months through August. The increase suggests that Indian manufacturers are beginning to supply components and intermediate products to China's industrial ecosystem, creating opportunities beyond finished goods assembled for Western markets. The potential for India to become a more integrated manufacturing partner is now in sight.
This shift could support investment in factories, components and industrial infrastructure. India's large workforce and domestic market add to its appeal as companies look for additional production bases.
Roubini's central argument is that India has done very well and is well placed to benefit from a changing global economy. The next few decades may indeed offer India an opportunity on a scale comparable to China's rise, with the country's policy choices helping determine how fully that opportunity is realised.

articles.summary: After beef feast near Dhaka temple, students plan cow slaughter during Durga Puja  India TodayAnti-India Slogans Raised After 'Beef Khichdi' Served Near Dhaka Temple  NDTVBeef khichuri row near Dhaka temple turns tense at Durga Puja, as students slaughter cow on campus  PGurusCow slaughtered at JnU campus, Socialist Students’ Front alleges communal intolerance  New Age BDBeef feast at JnU to protest slaughter ban  The Daily Star
articles.full_text:
A controversy over a beef khichuri event near a Hindu temple at Dhaka's Jagannath University has escalated. Some of the students are planning to slaughter cows on campus on Friday, coinciding with Durga Puja festivities. The row, which was triggered by the beef khichuri event and its opposition by Hindu students, has now intensified after the university issued a notice restricting animal slaughter, only to later clarify that students could organise such events.
A controversy over a beef khichuri event near a temple in Dhaka's Jagannath University in Dhaka has snowballed into a major dispute over religious sensitivities, campus rules and the rights of students to organise events. A group of Islamic history students has now announced plans to slaughter cows on the campus on Friday, October 16, coinciding with Durga Puja. Earlier, the university officials had issued a notice asking students to refrain from animal slaughter on the premises, which was later overturned.
The planned event on Friday coincides with Maha Shashthi, which marks the beginning of Durga Puja.
According to reports on BBC Bangla and The Daily Star, the dispute began on Monday, October 12, when students from the 17th batch (2021-22 academic session) of the Department of Islamic History and Culture organised a beef khicuri cookout near the university's Muktamancha (an open-air stage), close of the campus's central temple.
Hindu students subsequently objected to the location, saying it hurt their religious sentiments. Speaking to BBC Bangla, Joy Saha, member secretary of Jagganath University's' Central Temple Management Committee, stated that students approached the kichuri cookout organisers after discovering that beef was being cooked. He said the proximity to the temple caused distress and that they asked the organisers to move elsewhere.
A heated exchange followed before Professor Md Azam Khan intervened, sending an assistant proctor to calm things down. The feast organisers subsequently moved further from the temple, and stated that they had no intention of hurting anyone's religious sentiments.
DISPUTE OVER TEMPLE BRICKS
This, however, was not the end of the story. Allegations soon surfaced that the organisers of the cook-out had used bricks belonging to the temple to build a temporary oven to cook the beef khichuri.
According to a report by the Dhaka-based outlet, The Daily Star, the students who organised the cookout had initially planned to cook the khichuri in the university cafeteria itself. The plan was scuppered thanks to low cooking gas pressure and the organisers elected to shift to an outdoor location. While setting up a temporary oven, they ended up using bricks which they said they found nearby, unaware they belonged to the campus temple, said the event organisers.
The organisers later removed the bricks, brought an iron stove from the cafeteria and apologised for the misunderstanding, reported The Daily Star. However, Saha told BBC Bangla that the primary concern was the cooking arrangement's proximity to the temple, rather than the bricks.
In any case, the cat was out of the bag. The same night, aggrieved Hindu students staged a demonstration and formed a human chain, demanding an impartial enquiry and safeguards for religious shrines on campus, reported The Daily Star. Central Temple Management Committee Convener Ajoy Paul, meanwhile, was reported by the newspaper as calling for administrative action to protect the temple's sanctity and ensure communal harmony.
UNIVERSITY ISSUED TWO NOTICES
Following the October 12 dispute, officials at Jagannath University issued a notice on Wednesday, October 14, asking student, teachers and staff to refrain from slaughtering animals on campus grounds, citing the need to maintain a hygienic environment.
According to the BBC Bangla report, the notice referred to a Dhaka South City Corporation public notice concerning animal slaughter and meat regulation. Under Bangladesh's Animal Slaughter and Meat Quality Control Act, 2011, slaughter outside designated slaughterhouses is subject to legal restrictions, while violations can attract penalties.
The announcement triggered objections from some students, who viewed it as a restriction on their right to organise a beef feast, given the dispute that had transpired two days before.
Professor Azam Khan told BBC Bangla that the administration had issued the notice after learning of plans for animal slaughter. He said it wanted to prevent tensions from escalating during ongoing religious observances.
Later that day, the university issued a second notice clarifying its position. It said the original misunderstanding over the cookout had been resolved through the proctor's intervention and subsequent discussions between the parties.
The administration apologised for the misunderstanding caused by its earlier notice and said students had the right to organise events on campus, including those involving animal slaughter. However, it urged everyone to ensure that one group’s activities did not obstruct another’s.
STUDENTS ORGANISE BEEF FEAST IN PROTEST
The university's clarification that the notice to refrain from beef slaughter was not related to the dispute on October 12, failed to calm tempers. A group of students has now announced plans for a beef feast on Friday, October 16, describing it as a protest against the administration’s initial notice.
A member of the organising committee, speaking on condition of anonymity, told BBC Bangla that the students had initially considered holding the event after Durga Puja.
"Since there is so much anger over cows, we were thinking of organising a cow event after Durga Puja. But yesterday, when the administration issued a notice saying cows could not be slaughtered on campus, it hurt the students," the organiser said.
The organiser indicated that the event would likely take place in an open field near the Arts Building rather than beside the temple.
According to BBC Bangla, organisers have collected contributions and purchased a cow. Bangladesh Islamist Chhatra Majlis, a student organisation affiliated with the far-right Islamist party, the Khelafat Majlis, has also reportedly offered to provide another. Social media announcements invited participants to register for Taka 70.
Jagannath University Central Students’ Union General Secretary Abdul Alim Arif told BBC Bangla that student representatives had met university officials and reached an understanding that the event could proceed.
Proctor Azam Khan said the slaughter, if held, should be conducted in a restrained manner to prevent another dispute over religious sensitivities.
Saha also told BBC Bangla that the temple committee did not object to students slaughtering cows elsewhere on campus, provided the activity did not take place in front of the temple or disrupt its activities.
The university has urged students to respect one another’s religious practices and ensure that campus events do not interfere with others.

articles.title: Yogi Adityanath rejects Congress protests, calls Indian democracy a colossal banyan tree - The News Mill

Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath criticised opposition parties on October 16, asserting that in a democracy power is derived strictly from the electorate’s mandate rather than through street protests. He warned against attempts to replicate “Bangladesh-style” political upheavals in India.
In a post on social media platform X, the Chief Minister stated, “In a democracy, the path to power flows from the mandate of the people, not from chaos. Forces dreaming of a change of power in India on the lines of Bangladesh want to place the tools of anarchy in the hands of the youth instead of the torch of nation-building.”
Addressing ongoing demonstrations related to the Election Commission and voter list revisions, he described Indian democracy as an unshakeable institution. “Those sowing the seeds of instability in the country under the guise of electoral reform, the slogan of justice, and the invocation of democracy must understand that India’s democracy is a colossal banyan tree rooted in public trust, which cannot be shaken by the tempests of conspiracies,” he said.
Targeting the leaders of the protests, Adityanath added that the country’s youth would not be used as instruments for narrow political ambitions. “Our youth power is for shaping India’s future, not for quenching anyone’s thirst for power. The people have recognised these mirages and villains in politics and kept them away from power. Now, they seek to seize the chair by plunging the country into the fire of anarchy. The nation will never allow this political conspiracy of theirs to succeed,” he affirmed.
These remarks followed strong criticism from senior Bharatiya Janata Party leaders, including Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who accused the opposition of orchestrating a coordinated “politics of disruption” across Delhi.
Earlier on the same day, at a press conference in Lucknow, Rajnath Singh said, “The developments that have taken place in Delhi over the past few days raise several serious questions. It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos.”
He added, “Attempts are being made to use the nation’s youth as pawns in a politics of chaos. Some seek a regime change—modelled after the events in Bangladesh—openly admitting that they drew inspiration from the situation in Bangladesh; others, meanwhile, brazenly call for the toppling of the government. This makes it clear that their sole agenda is to dismantle democratic institutions and set the country ablaze…their struggle is not for electoral reform, nor is it about SIR or Gyanesh Kumar; it is not for the sake of a bright future for the nation’s youth—rather, it is a conspiracy to seize power by inciting anarchy in the country.”
The comments come amid ongoing protests by opposition leaders, INDIA bloc parties, and student organisations against the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
