The shift in supply sources has helped India, Japan and Korea bring oil flows back to the levels recorded before the conflict. The IMF attributed this recovery partly to the countries' ability to secure supplies from outside the Middle East.
“For other large Asian economies (including India, Japan, and Korea), the resilience in part reflects adaptation by securing oil from alternative sources outside the Middle East,” the report said. It added that total oil flows to these countries had returned to their pre-conflict rates since June.
Refined fuel prices add to cost pressures
The pressure on energy costs has not been uniform across products. The IMF noted that refined petroleum products, particularly diesel and jet fuel, had recorded sharper price increases than crude oil following the conflict.
If these costs remain high, businesses could face increased transportation and production expenses, with the impact potentially extending to consumers. The report warned that a prolonged conflict could keep energy prices elevated and sustain wider commodity price pressures.
Higher energy bills pose a fiscal challenge
Expensive energy could also leave governments across the region with less room to manage their finances while providing relief to households facing higher costs. The IMF warned that rising energy prices could worsen fiscal balances, making it harder to protect vulnerable sections of the population without undermining fiscal sustainability.
The report recommended that governments focus on targeted assistance rather than measures that apply broadly across the economy. “Fiscal policy should prioritize preserving sustainability while protecting vulnerable households,” it said, advocating targeted and time-bound support instead of broad-based fuel subsidies or price controls.
AI investments and global financial conditions among other risks
The IMF also pointed to uncertainty over artificial intelligence investments and tighter global financial conditions as potential sources of pressure on regional growth.
A correction in AI-related investments or asset valuations could weigh on business investment and private consumption. Separately, higher global sovereign yields could spill over into regional bond markets, adding to the challenges facing Asian economies.
The IMF has projected India's GDP growth at 7% in 2026 and 2027, with private consumption and services activity expected to support expansion. However, managing external shocks and maintaining macroeconomic stability will remain important to sustaining this growth.
To strengthen the region's ability to withstand future disruptions, the IMF called for improvements in energy security, investment in digital infrastructure and skills, and policies focused on price stability.

A federal court has ordered the US government to allow up to 55,000 people from across countries to apply for Green Card. District Judge Jinsook Ohta directed the Department of State to reopen the diversity visa lottery for 2027, popularly known as the Green Card lottery. The e Trump administration opposes the program and did not open the registration period on time for this year. It subsequently argued that it was too late to do so. In the latest order, Ohta directed Secretary of State 
Marco Rubio
 to reopen the registration period for the lottery. The verdict comes after Red Eagle Law filed a lawsuit against Rubio in August this year.
What the court said
In the order, judge Jinsook Ohta said “The announcement shall identify the opening and closing dates of the registration period, the website through which individuals may submit electronic entries, and the requirements for participating in the program”.
“Defendant shall further disseminate this information through the State Department’s other customary public notification channels, including the Federal Register,” he further wrote.
Ohta ruled that the registration period should last 30 days. The ruling also requires the State Department to accept electronic entries submitted during the registration period, given that applicants meet eligibility and documentation requirements.
Additionally, it requires the State Department to notify individuals who are selected for the diversity visa lottery and process their applications under its usual procedures.
US immigration authority changes rules of green card applications
Earlier this year, US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) announced a new policy under which foreigners applying for permanent residency in the US will now have to go back to their home countries to seek Green Cards. “From now on, an alien who is in the US temporarily and wants a green card must return to their home country to apply, except in extraordinary circumstances,” Zach Kahler, a spokesman for US Citizenship and Immigration Services, said in a statement.
USCIS announced the move in a policy memo, which then directed officers to consider relevant factors and information on a case-by-case basis when determining whether extraordinary relief is warranted. "An alien who is in the U.S. temporarily and wants a Green Card must return to their home country to apply," said the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which has oversight of USCIS. Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury has said Bangladesh and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will hold further discussions for two weeks from next week to work out the details of the country's loan proposal, with the aim of finalising the outstanding issues.
"In principle, everything is fine. Now, the two teams will sit together to discuss how to close the deal," he said after a meeting with the IMF in Bangkok today (16 October).

All multilateral organisations are working closely with Bangladesh, he said, adding that all multilateral and bilateral partners, including the World Bank, IMF, Asian Development Bank and Japan International Cooperation Agency, are keen to support the country.

articles.title: The debt trap: How unsecured credit is silently reshaping young India’s financial future - Ideas for India
articles.summary: The debt trap: How unsecured credit is silently reshaping young India’s financial future  Ideas for India
articles.full_text:
India’s household debt-to-GDP ratio is on the rise – driven in part by youth borrowing for skill acquisition, basic living expenses, and lifestyle consumption. In this post, R Stuthi Raja cautions that such an economic model erodes the financial resilience of the emerging middle class and delays long-term capital formation. She recommends reforming education finance, safeguarding entry-level wage growth, and embedding architectural regulatory friction into digital consumer credit.
When previous generations of Indians spoke of debt, they spoke of it in hushed, hesitant tones. Borrowing was a measure of last resort, a heavy burden borne in mid-life to finance a first home, a child’s higher education, or an unexpected medical crisis. Today, that cultural taboo has dissolved into a single tap on a smartphone screen.
This cultural shift marks a broader macroeconomic transformation in household finance. Credit in modern India no longer functions primarily as a tool for long-term physical asset creation; it increasingly fuels daily consumption and workforce preparation. As millions of young adults adopt frictionless digital credit, this micro-level debt overhang suppresses future macroeconomic growth. According to the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Financial Stability Report, India’s household debt-to-GDP (gross domestic product) ratio has reached 45.5%, rising well above its five-year average of 38.3%. Data from Business Standard confirms this demographic shift: 53% of Indians take their first personal loan before age 30, while 57% obtain their first credit card before turning 30.
None of this makes credit the problem. Household consumption is the largest component of India’s economy: private final consumption expenditure reached 61.5% of GDP in 2025-26, its highest share since 2011-12, according to the Economic Survey 2025-26. Borrowing that supports this spending can strengthen growth when it builds skills, raises earning power, or creates assets that hold their value. It works against growth when households use it to finance things that lose value faster than the loan is repaid, because the debt outlives what it bought and pulls income away from savings and future spending.
Addressing the surge in youth borrowing requires moving beyond broad digital lending guidelines. Treating all unsecured credit through a single regulatory lens misdiagnoses the crisis. Easy credit is not merely funding impulsive spending; it is compensating for stagnant entry-level wages, shifting the cost of human capital development onto young workers, and exploiting vulnerabilities in digital credit architecture. To craft effective interventions, policymakers must recognise that young India navigates three distinct categories of debt: productive, survival, and indulgence, each rooted in a different economic dynamic requiring a tailored policy framework.
Productive debt: Reforming higher education financing
At the foundational level lies productive debt, borrowing undertaken to build human capital and expand future earning potential. Long before applying for their first consumer credit card or purchasing electronics on instalment, millions of young adults enter the workforce pre-encumbered by substantial educational debt. As higher education has transitioned from a publicly subsidised good to a privatised financial market, tuition fees have far outpaced inflation.
Data from The Federal reveal that total active education loan portfolios in India have exceeded Rs. 1.37 trillion. Escalating university costs have forced a structural shift toward an earn-and-study model, where students take on education loans for professional degrees and depend on entry-level jobs primarily to service these obligations. With commercial education loan interest rates ranging from 8.25% to 15%, as documented by Ruloans, new graduates enter the labour market with high, fixed debt-servicing commitments before earning their first rupee of discretionary income.
This structural burden exposes a fundamental policy misalignment in higher education financing. While higher education generates long-term tax revenues and economic productivity for the nation, commercial lenders treat study loans as high-risk consumer credit. Evaluating human capital development strictly through private risk commercialises what is fundamentally a public good.
To prevent student debt from depressing early-career savings capacity and delaying future capital formation, policy frameworks should cap education loan interest rates to the benchmark sovereign bond yield rate, the baseline risk-free cost of borrowing in the economy (currently hovering around 6.75-6.8%). Indexing student credit directly to sovereign yields aligns education finance with Central Bank monetary policy and State credit guarantees, ensuring capital flows into skill-building without subjecting young graduates to private credit margins.
Survival debt: Safeguarding early-career wage growth
While education loans represent an investment in future earning power, survival borrowing reflects immediate economic friction within the labour market. As moderate inflation collides with near-flat real wage growth – which has stagnated around 0-1% annually across urban, manufacturing, and informal – entry-level compensation has decoupled from the cost of living in major employment hubs.
The RBI’s Financial Stability report June 2026, finds that three-fourths of unsecured retail loans originate from individuals earning under Rs. 10 lakh annually. Faced with high urban rents, commuting expenses, and monthly education loan EMIs (equal monthly instalments), entry-level professionals routinely use credit cards and short-term micro-loans to cover basic monthly necessities like groceries and utilities.
In economic terms, the reliance on unsecured credit to meet basic living costs represents a structural labour market distortion: short-term debt has effectively become a de facto wage substitute. By absorbing the gap between stagnant entry-level compensation and high urban living costs, digital credit provides an implicit subsidy to employers, allowing corporate wage growth to decouple from productivity. This reliance creates a broader debt overhang that drains household discretionary income, depresses net national savings, and delays long-term capital formation among young workforce entrants, ultimately converting India's demographic dividend into a systemic balance-sheet risk.
Addressing survival debt requires strengthening early-career labour market governance. By establishing localised wage-floor benchmarks, regulating off-contract probation periods, and enforcing compensation transparency for entry-level and trainee roles. Mandating fair, cost-indexed entry-level compensation frameworks and eliminating uncompensated training periods ensures that early-career professionals can meet baseline urban living costs through earned income rather than debt reliance.
Indulgence debt: Architecting friction in digital consumer credit
At the opposite end of the spectrum sits digital consumer credit, driven by aspirational consumption and accelerated by digital platforms. Young borrowers utilise credit cards, Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) schemes, and algorithmic micro-loans to finance short-term discretionary dining, travel, and lifestyle upgrades. A survey by mPokket indicates that 63% of young Indians view credit cards as tools for financial control, reflecting a low-friction attitude toward taking on consumer debt.
Algorithmic fintech platforms serve as the primary delivery infrastructure for this trend. By eliminating traditional banking procedures, fintech apps deliver unsecured capital in under 24 hours without requiring collateral. Data from TransUnion CIBIL show that 61% of digital fintech borrowers are under age 30. According to CRIF High Mark, the active fintech loan portfolio reached ₹2.1 trillion in June 2025. Separately, RBI data show that outstanding credit-card debt reached ₹2.91 lakh crore in July 2025.
However, instant liquidity comes with high interest costs. Annualised percentage rates on fintech micro-loans frequently range between 10-30%, compounded by processing fees and late penalties. As short-term liquidity tightens, micro-loan stacks unravel rapidly: LiveMint reports that loans overdue by more than 180 days in the fintech segment rose from 7.1% in 2024 to 8.6% in 2025, signaling mounting default stress among first-time borrowers.
Digital consumer credit represents an unhedged expansion of unsecured lending that alters household balance sheet dynamics. By providing instant liquidity, algorithmic fintech platforms accelerate the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) among young demographics, allowing them to finance short-term discretionary spending against anticipated future earnings. While this credit expansion smooths immediate retail demand, high annualised interest rates and fee structures create an intertemporal debt overhang. Over time, this overhang dampens long-term aggregate demand as an increasing share of future disposable income shifts toward servicing debt rather than funding future consumption or savings.
Beyond dampening retail demand, uncollateralised digital lending introduces systemic risk to the formal banking sector. Because fintech platforms frequently originate loans through co-lending partnerships, First-Loss Default Guarantees (FLDG), and credit lines from institutional lenders, consumer default stress does not remain contained within digital startups. In the absence of real-time, cross-platform exposure tracking, borrowers facing liquidity shortfalls engage in multi-app "loan stacking" by using new digital credit lines to service existing obligations. This practice generates rapid credit contagion. When liquidity tightens, default rates rise, accelerating the accumulation of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) across partnering commercial banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs).
